#6388. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part III: The Legacy of Frank Drake & Carl Sagan

Welcome back to our continuing series on the Brief-ish History of METI, where we examine the rise, development, and possible implications of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our first installment, we explored some of the foundational principles, how METI emerged as a possible answer to the "SETI Paradox," and the earliest experiments. In our second, we looked at the pioneering work of Cornell Professor Frank Drake, the "father of SETI," and how his efforts led to the first true experiment in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI): Project Ozma and the Arecibo Message.

We also touched on how these efforts led to his lifelong collaboration with fellow Cornell Professor and famed science communicator Carl Sagan. Today, we will see how this collaboration attracted the attention of NASA and led to the most ambitious projects to send messages to space, ones that might even be found by an extraterrestrial civilization (ETC) someday. These are none other than the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records, which are now in the outer Solar System or have entered interstellar space.

As noted in our last installment, Carl Sagan and Frank Drake first met in 1961, a year after Project Ozma took place. To build on the momentum the experiment created, Drake organized an informal symposium at the Green Bank Observatory (where Ozma was conducted) in 1961. To prepare for the event, Drake formulated an equation that summarized the challenges SETI researchers faced. This became known as the Drake Equation, which remains foundational to the fields of SETI and METI.

The equation states that the number of extraterrestrial civilizations in our galaxy that we could communicate with (N) depends on several variables. These include the annual rate of star formation in the galaxy (R*), the fraction of those stars with planets (fp), the number of planets with conditions suitable for life (ne), the fraction of planets that will develop intelligence (fi), the fraction of planets with intelligent life that will develop transmission technologies (fc), and the average length of time a civilization will be able to produce signals (L). Mathematically, the equation is expressed as:

As one of many prominent scientists attending the symposium, Sagan was impressed with Drake's theories and advocacy for using radio astronomy to search for possible ETCs. However, their interactions predated this meeting and included correspondence when both were young graduate astronomy students. Sagan became aware of Drake when he heard of his work measuring Venus's high temperature. After this meeting, the two became close colleagues and professors at Cornell University, where they went on to collaborate on several landmark projects.

In the early 1970s, the last Apollo mission successfully landed astronauts on the Moon (Eugene A. Cernan, Harrison H. Schmitt, and Ronald E. Evans). This historic accomplishment effectively ended the "Space Race," and NASA was busy contemplating its next moves. It was decided that the Pioneer program, which had sent nine probes to explore the Moon, Venus, Mars, and Mercury between 1958 and 1968, should shift focus to the outer Solar System, exploring the Main Asteroid Belt, Jupiter, Saturn, and the interstellar medium.

This made the probes especially significant, as they would be the first missions to achieve escape velocity from the Solar System. For this reason, journalist and science correspondent Eric Burgess (who was also the Pioneer program's chronicler) suggested that the probes carry a message, should an extraterrestrial species find them someday. Burgess approached Carl Sagan with the idea after hearing him lecture about communicating with extraterrestrial intelligence at a conference in Crimea.

Sagan was enthusiastic about the idea and approached Frank Drake to help design a message that could be interpreted by an ETC. NASA agreed to the plan and gave them three weeks to prepare it, and the two decided to create plaques that could be mounted on the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions. Linda Salzman Sagan, Carl Sagan's wife at the time, prepared the artwork, with additional contributions from space artist and science journalist Jon Lomberg, a long-time collaborator of Sagan's.

The result was the Pioneer Plaques, a pair of six-by-nine-inch (~23 cm by 15.25 cm) gold-anodized aluminum plates. Each contained an engraved pictorial message identifying the probes' place of origin, who sent them, and when they were sent. From top to bottom, left to right, the message included the following details:

A detailed view of the visual message on the Pioneer plaques, developed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake. Credit: NASA Ames

The Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 probes launched on March 2nd, 1972, and April 5th, 1973 (respectively), becoming the first robotic missions to explore beyond Mars and the Main Asteroid Belt. The Pioneer Plaques have the distinction of being humanity's first interstellar message of greetings. But in a few years' time, Sagan and Drake would take things a step further, creating something that was meant to convey what life on Earth was like.

The success of the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions motivated NASA to contemplate an even more ambitious mission: dual probes to explore the planets of the outer Solar System. The twin Voyager 1 and 2 probes would launch in the summer of 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment of the outer planets. The mission would conduct close-up studies of Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn's rings, and larger moons. But as the mission progressed, NASA chose to use the alignment to include Uranus and Neptune - what came to be known as the "Grand Tour."

Since these missions would also achieve escape velocity from the Solar System, NASA decided to follow the precedent established with the Pioneer Plaques. This led Voyager project manager John R. Casani to suggest that the Voyager 1 and 2 probes also carry a "message in a bottle" containing information about humanity. He delegated the task to Carl Sagan, who was joined again by Frank Drake and Linda Salzman Sagan, and the three created a metal phonograph record containing information encoded in its grooves.

A record was chosen because it would outlast magnetic tape in the outer-space environment. This time, Sagan and crew were given six weeks to create the records and a budget of $1,500, the equivalent of about 8,780 USD today, though Sagan and his colleagues contributed money of their own. The fruits of their labors were the Voyager Golden Records, a series of 12-inch (30.5 cm) gold-plated copper disks containing sounds and images that portrayed the diversity of life and culture on Earth.

The outer cases were etched with pictograms (see above) similar to the Pioneer Plaques, showing where the probes came from. They also contained instructions for playing the record. In the upper left corner of the case, there is a drawing of the phonograph record and the stylus in the correct position for playing it. Around it, conveyed in binary arithmetic, are the time it takes for the record to complete one rotation (3.6 seconds), the total duration (1 hour), and how it should be played from the outside in.

The upper-right corner contains instructions for constructing pictures from the record. From top to bottom, these include a representation of the signal that indicates the start of a picture, how the signals must be grouped as a series of 512 vertical lines per picture, and what the first image looks like (a circle) to confirm the signals are being processed correctly. The drawing in the lower left-hand corner of the cover is the pulsar map (similar to the Pioneer Plaques) and a drawing of the hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen.

The Voyager Golden Record (right) and its protective casing with instructions on how to play along with information about its origin (left). Credit: NASA

The record contains 115 encoded images that show human anatomy (a silhouette of a man and a pregnant woman), the structure of DNA, demonstrations of eating and drinking, major locations on Earth, sports and leisure, our planet's geography, and mathematical/scientific concepts. It also contains sound recordings of greetings in 55 languages, whale calls, and music from various cultures and eras (including Beethoven and Chuck Berry). Said then-President Jimmy Carter of the Records:

This is a present from a small, distant world, a token of our sounds, our science, our images, our music, our thoughts and our feelings. We are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours.

The cover also features a "radioactive clock" in the form of an electroplated uranium-238 sample. Since this element has a half-life of 4.51 billion years, the recipients can calculate how long the probe has been in space. Unlike the Pioneer Plaques, the Voyager Golden Records had a dual purpose: as a message to any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted them, or as a time capsule for future generations of human explorers should they find them first. As Sagan noted at the time:

The spacecraft will be encountered, and the record played only if there are advanced spacefaring civilizations in interstellar space, but the launching of this 'bottle' into the cosmic 'ocean' says something very hopeful about life on this planet.

Based on its current trajectory and velocity, Pioneer 10 will reach Aldebaran, a star roughly 65 light-years away in the Taurus constellation, in over two million years. Meanwhile, Pioneer 11 is headed for the Aquila constellation and will pass near one of its stars in about 4 million years. On August 25th, 2012, Voyager 1 made history by becoming the first probe to exit the heliosphere and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2 exited from a different location on November 5th, 2018, becoming the second.

They will be joined by Pioneer 10 and 11 probes around 2057, though this will be difficult to verify since both probes are unpowered and cannot send data back to Earth. These plaques and records are unique in that they remain humanity's first attempts to send physical messages into space intended for extraterrestrial recipients and/or future generations. They also established a legacy that continues to this day and is part of a larger debate surrounding the ethics of METI.

This illustration shows the positions of NASA's Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes outside the heliosphere, a protective bubble created by the Sun that extends well past Pluto's orbit. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

These missions have also inspired debate about what a modern message should be and have inspired some experiments. In a series of NASA-led studies that appeared in the AGU journal Earth and Space Science, an international team of scientists proposed what a modern Golden Record should contain. In the first study, titled "Message in a BottleâAn Update to the Golden Record: 1. Objectives and Key Content of the Message," the team summarized the importance of the "Message In A Bottle" (MIAB) and what should motivate future efforts:

These records not only offer a snapshot of Earth and human civilization but also represent our desire to establish contact with advanced alien civilizations. Our goal is to share our collective knowledge, emotions, innovations, and aspirations in a way that provides a universal, yet contextually relevant, understanding of human society, the evolution of life on Earth, and our hopes and concerns for the future. Through this time and space traveling capsule, we also strive to inspire and unify current and future generations to celebrate and safeguard our shared human experience.

Modern attempts to fashion a MIAB include the message attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to rendezvous with Jupiter and study its moon Europa. The message was unveiled in March 2024, about seven months before the mission launched, and consists of a triangular tantalum plaque - known as the Europa Clipper Vault Plate - measuring about 18 x 28 cm (about 7 x 11 inches) that features graphic elements on both sides. The inward-facing side features an engraving of U.S. Poet Laureate Ada LimÃ³n's handwritten "In Praise of Mystery: A Poem for Europa."

The outward-facing panel contains etchings of soundwaves that illustrate Earth's connection to Europa. Each etching is the word "water" spoken in one of 103 languages from around the world, which were converted into waveforms. Each waveform radiates outward from a symbol representing the sign for "water" in American Sign Language (ASL). Since the Europa Clipper is searching for possible evidence of life inside the icy moon, the Drake Equation is also etched into the plate.

Rather than being a message intended for extraterrestrials, this "Golden Record for Europa" honors the spirit of the original records, aiming to spark the imagination and offer a unifying vision. As Lori Glaze, director of the Planetary Science Division at NASA, said in a statement:

The content and design of Europa Clipper's vault plate are swimming with meaning. The plate combines the best humanity has to offer across the universe â science, technology, education, art, and math. The message of connection through water, essential for all forms of life as we know it, perfectly illustrates Earth's tie to this mysterious ocean world we are setting out to explore.

The "Message in a Bottle" plate attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to Jupiter. Credit: NASA

These messages highlight the major shift in consciousness that accompanied the Space Age. With humans now venturing out into space and exploring beyond Earth's orbit, a new awareness was taking root, one which saw humanity in cosmological terms. We were not only pondering the existence of extraterrestrial intelligence and civilizations. We were also considering how we might communicate with them and fashioning messages that might someday reach them... unless we get to them first!

These messages also raise the question of whether ETCs might be doing the same: could advanced civilizations be sending probes with their own messages, ones that share what life is like on their respective homeworlds? The fact that we have sent out four MIABs to date has motivated some scientists to consider the possibility that space is littered with derelict spacecraft, some of which could be messenger probes. Perhaps some of them are even here in our Solar System, lingering near Earth or in the far expanse of the Kuiper Belt.

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

#6387. Euclid's First Data Release: A Stepping Stone to its 3D Map of the Sky

The ESA's Euclid has already teased us with some early results. In the past it's given us a small, 60 square degree of the sky created with a few days of observations. Those images showed individual targets from the Horsehead Nebula to the Perseus cluster of galaxies.

But now we have data from more than one year of the telescope's observations, named DR1-Foundation. DR-1 Foundation covers a sky area as large as about 9,500 full moons, and captures light from more than one billion objects. It took about 13 months to gather all this data.

Understanding dark energy and dark matter means studying as much of the Universe as possible. The effects of dark energy and dark matter are felt at large scales, and by constructing an image of galaxy superclusters and the filaments they exist on, as well as the voids between those filaments, Euclid will lead to new understandings of both dark energy and dark matter.

There are other efforts to map this structure, some dating back decades. DESI, the Dark Energy Survey Instrument, has created the largest 3D map so far, but Euclid's will be larger. Euclid's will have more depth and volume, and since it's space-based while DESI is ground-based, it won't have to deal with atmospheric interference and will have a higher resolution.

This data release is from the Euclid's Wide and Deep Surveys, two surveys that will form the backbone of its 3D map. Even though the data covers 1900 square degrees of the sky, they only represent about 14% of the sky the space telescope will cover in its six-year mission.

This image shows Euclid's Wide Survey in light yellow and its Deep Survey in darker yellow. The Deep Survey are targeted regions within the Wide Survey. They're overlain on a star map from Gaia and a dust map from Planck. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA; ESA/Gaia/DPAC; ESA/Planck Collaboration. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

The Wide Survey is Euclid's primary campaign and will cover almost half of the galactic sky. It's an imaging and spectrographic survey in visible and near-infrared. It's the telescope's main cosmology survey and will cover a large volume to constrain dark energy and dark matter.

The Deep Survey serves a different purpose. It'll find fainter objects like dwarf galaxies, low-mass galaxies, and tidal tails, as well as high redshift galaxies and quasars. It will serve to calibrate the Wide Survey, and will provide its own, separate science based on its higher density of sources.

Basically, the Wide Durvey provides the greater volume, and the Deep Survey looks more closely and gives more depth. The two combined are needed for a cosmological survey.

Part of the release includes Euclid's image of the core of the Messier 81 galaxy group. This image shows part of that, centered on the Messier 81 galaxy, the group's largest member. The smaller NGC 3077 is on the left, which is also a member, as are many other small members spread across the image. Wispy blue clouds, sometimes called 'galactic cirrus clouds' are also visible. An irregular dwarf galaxy is also visible in diffuse blue to the left. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

Euclid also delivered an image of NGC 1291, a stunning ring galaxy about 33 million light years away. It's also called the Golden Eye galaxy, and it has an inner ring and an outer ring, as well as an inner bar. It's inner and outer rings may be because of a merger with a gas-rich galaxy in the past.

This is Euclid's image of NGC 1291, a ring galaxy that faces us head-on. It's about 33 million light years away, and highlights Euclid's power. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

Euclid also captured images of Abell 3128. It's 800 million light years away and contains hundreds of individual galaxies. Massive clusters like this one are important probes for dark energy and dark matter, but especially for dark matter. They serve as important gravitational lenses and reveal a lot about where dark matter is concentrated. They can help cosmologists test Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang theory of the Universe. They also help Euclid calibrate itself.

This is the Abell 3128 cluster, part of the Horologium supercluster. Horologium is home to more than 30 smaller clusters, and Abell 3128 is one of its richest members. Abell holds spirals and ellipticals, and a gravitational lens is in the middle, warping and magnifying the light from a distant background galaxy. The image shows only a fraction of Abell 3128, and also part of another galaxy cluster named ACT-CL J0330-5227; while in reality the two clusters are separated by a huge distance of around 5 billion light-years, they overlap here in our line of sight. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

We're only at the appetizer of the visual and scientific feast that Euclid will deliver. By the time it's completed, its 3D map of the sky will be visually entrancing and full of science. It's already discovered a new comet, the most ancient quasar in the Universe, and new images of the Milky Way's over-populated center.

It's off to a strong start and will only get better.

You can explore previous images from Euclid's 2024 Early Release Observations (ERO) and its Quick Euclid data release 1 (Q1) from 2025 at ESA Sky.

Evan Gough is a science-loving guy with no formal education who loves Earth, forests, hiking, and heavy music. He's guided by Carl Sagan's quote: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

#6386. What a 43-Year-Old Server and Drag Queen Eats on $63 CAN in Toronto, Ontario

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one anonymous reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today's Receipt, we follow a 43-year-old server and drag queen in Toronto, Ontario. Keep reading for his receipts.

The financesThe dietThe expensesThe diary

What is your occupation? Server, Drag Queen

What city and state do you live in? Toronto, ON

What is your annual salary, if you have one? Girl, I have no idea. Waiting tables brings in around $60K CAN, and performing in bars, nightclubs and drag brunches probably makes me another $3K, but all those sweat and glitter covered bills get stuffed under a mattress, so who knows?

How much is one paycheck, after taxes? Let’s call it an even thousand dollars.

How often are you paid? (e.g., weekly) Weekly or bi-weekly

What are your approximate fixed monthly expenses beyond food? (i.e., rent, subscriptions, bills)

Do you follow a certain diet or have dietary restrictions? I avoid salt and gluten as much as possible

What are the grocery staples you always buy, if any? Eggs, gluten-free pasta, bananas, bone broth, greens, yogurt. I almost always have boiled eggs ready in the fridge, a tub of yogurt, some dark berries, and bananas to keep me fueled up. If I’m going to cook, it’s pasta or meat and veggies.

How often in a week do you dine out versus cook at home? I work in an upscale Italian restaurant and the food is exceptional. I eat there 3 or 4 times a week and have the cholesterol levels to prove it. At 50% off any menu items (minus the $128 porterhouse steak) it’s a bargain to eat delicious, mostly healthy cooked meals. I love going out socially or alone, and do so almost weekly.

How often in a week did you dine out while growing up? Once a month? Rural Alberta didn’t have a ton of dining out choices

How often in a week did your parents or guardians cook at home? Daily. My mom’s (and occasionally my dad’s) cooking was excellent. Nothing fancy, but a real meat-and-potatoes type menu that kept us going

10 a.m. My annual sinus infection came early, and I’ve been sick since Saturday. I’m trying to break my morning caffeine habit, but today I’m too lazy and run down. I hydrate with lemon water while sipping an Americano with brown sugar. Between the coffee and the illness I don’t have much of an appetite. I forage on peanut butter and pumpkin seeds while shuffling around my apartment.

4 p.m. A thought occurs to me: Let’s heal this body with some miso and wasabi. I order sushi from Kibo down the street. It’s take-out, so I am forced to don clothing and walk down the street. I pick up 2-for-1 dynamite rolls, chicken gyoza dumplings, miso soup, the obligatory green salad that comes with it all. and a spicy salmon combo. $44

As I’m feeling sorry for myself on my walk back home, I stop at the corner store for a bottle of Blake Boulevard Sauvignon Blanc. $21

10 a.m. I know that I have a shift at the restaurant today, so I'm holding my head up and pretending that I'm not at death's door. A banana and blueberry yogurt provide the gas I need to leave the house to get provisions.

We’re out of coffee beans! I have two espresso machines because I am a complete coffee snob. Machine number 1, my favorite, is a DeLonghi manual espresso maker, a tall, silver tower with a handle on the side. I grind my own beans for this. Machine number 2 is a Nespresso Virtuo. It requires aluminum pods stuffed with coffee. It’s sleek and makes a lovely crema, but it’s never hot enough for me. The pods vary between $1.12 and $1.50 each.

On the way home I stop in at St. Clair Avenue Fruit Market for some of my usuals: bok choy, celery, dates, rapini, bananas, and a container of feta, for fun. $31.75

3 p.m. Before work I load up on cold meds even though they make me feel like a bobble head. Somewhere between 4PM and 7PM I ask my chef to sneak me some arancini to avoid passing out while bringing some nice folks their wine and dinner. Our arancini are filled with mozzarella, rolled in a saffron risotto and plated with tomato sauce. Retail $24, but for me it’s $12.

10 a.m. Americano, brown sugar, lemon water. I have a friend coming in from out of town and she is fully aware how ill I am, and I feel as though she may need a snack after her 2+ hour drive, so I pop down to another cute hot spot on my street, Le Bleu. I may or may not also have a huge crush on the owner, Iman. I pick up vegan baklava, vegan banana bread, a Caprese sandwich for her and prosciutto for me. I try to make small talk with Iman while he packs up my order, but he’s so handsome I end up muttering and mumbling my thank yous while I stumble out the door. $25.76

6 p.m. Reservations for 2 at a vegetarian restaurant, Planta, Toronto, in Yorkville. I am not a vegetarian. I had mid to low expectations. Guys, this place was incredible.

Delicious regular and zero-proof cocktails. A “Cosmic Colada” for me: Coconut water, lemon, blueberry and pineapple. For my friend: the Tokyo Blossom made with sake, gin, lychee liquor and grapefruit tonic.

The unagi eggplant was so good I almost ordered a second one; we also ordered spicy tuna roll (some kind of juiced-up watermelon substitution), miso soup, and bang bang broccoli. I ordered a chocolate brownie and a sticky toffee pudding for dessert—the latter was so big it was almost comical. They also stuffed an entire ice cream cone full of vanilla ice cream upside down onto my pudding. I finished about a quarter of it.

After she leaves and the day progresses I realize I am in no shape to work. Thankfully someone takes my serving shift so I don’t have to go and cough all over our lovely patrons.

6 p.m. My appetite has been suffering, but eventually I whip up one of my favorites: a bean medley, chickpea, celery, olive oil and feta salad.

8 p.m. As the sun sets and the self pity sinks in deeper, I throw a trench coat over my pajamas and scurry down to the store to get another favorite, a bottle of Te Henga Sauvignon Blanc. $19.45

10 a.m. Another Americano and lemon water.

1 p.m. At this point in the week I am so sick of tea I never want to see it again. I’ve been trying to stave off whatever I have with honey/lemon/ginger tea and I’m over it. That was lunch, I guess.

8 p.m. Guilty pleasure time! I call in an order for Little Caesars Chicago Deep Dish Meat Treat pizza, an order of hot wings, and a ginger ale. Pure class and total nutrition. The good news is that while attempting to remain unseen, I happen to run into someone I’ve been chatting with on a dating app. Oh did I say good? I meant horrific. $39.77

10 a.m. Americano. Lemon Water. I’m a creature of habit, ok?

12 p.m. Bananas, blueberries, leftover bean salad, ginger tea.

3 p.m. I’m at work early, because we have new menu items. At pre-shift, the chef makes one of each and we discuss and sample it. A prime rib chuck burger with scamorza and tomato bomba, lamb pizza with basil pesto, steak tartare, Atlantic cod and potato risotto, and mushroom and pea stuffed ravioli. Some call this “product knowledge.” I call it a free meal(s).

8:45 p.m. Despite all my newfound product knowledge, I still get hungry halfway through my shift. Chef makes me a bulgur, kale, and roasted beet salad with a 7oz flatiron steak. $22

10:45 p.m. Shift done, head feeling like a block of ice, I sneak off to the market before heading home to grab a bottle of Squealing Pig Sauvignon Blanc. $22

10 a.m. Pretty much right after I open my eyes I get a lovely text from a friend; “Wanna get breakfast?” She knows I’ve been sick and we haven’t caught up in a while. She is informed that I will be wearing my now-uniform of pajamas and trench coat.

11 a.m. Three eggs, toast, and bacon from a pub by my house. No culinary awards will be given out here but it did what it was supposed to do. The bill for both meals with coffee and a couple of spicy Bloody Caesars came to $50.

7 p.m. Another go-to when I’m feeling down or simply have the craving is to simmer some rice noodles in a broth and add miso paste. I stir in fresh chopped bok choy, green onions and a couple of cut-up hard boiled eggs. I think I’m gonna make it.

#6385. The Restaurants Already on Eater Editors’ Radar for 2027

These restaurants are already creating buzz

Editors’ scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, wrapped up at the end of August — just as fall restaurant-opening season was heating up. That means several notable restaurants that debuted in 2026 didn’t quite make the cut, either because they didn’t open in time or had only been open a matter of weeks and were still finding their footing as of our deadline. But that just gives us a place to start on next year’s research. Here are some early contenders on our radar — places we’re thrilled to have in the conversation no matter how the scene shakes up as 2026 wraps and we continue into 2027.

Our New York team is excited to see the full spectrum of what pastry chef Camari Mick has in store with her own new venture, Afro-Caribbean brasserie and bakery Calabash, which opened in the West Village in early October.

Also in the West Village, the Taqueria Ramírez team debuted this Mexican-seafood-focused wine bar, which translates to “the hairy shrimp.” The tiny convivial space opened in mid-September.

Alex McCoy’s resurrected Thai restaurant, which opened in early September, is dishing up some of the spiciest Thai food the D.C. area has seen since the much-lamented closure of Little Serow. The alleyway hot spot in Georgetown is drawing crowds for its monkfish curry, khao soi, and natural wine list. Thanks to its moody, candlelit atmosphere, it’s also becoming a favorite tucked-away date spot.

Chicago’s tavern-style pizza has been having a moment outside of the Midwest; in D.C., it’s a menu centerpiece of La Merna, which has been one of the city’s tough-to-get tables since its August opening. Co-owner Bradley Shorten used to run a few tavern-style pizzerias in Chicago, and his wife and partner Meg Schmitt, who has a background in cheese distribution, is topping pastas with cheeses she makes fresh. The wood-paneled dining room with red leather-covered booths resembles a Midwest supper club with its laid-back, old-school atmosphere.

We had high hopes that this coastal Italian Pittsburgh restaurant — from the team behind Lilith, Jamilka Borges and Dianne DeStefano — would open in time for 2026 Eater Awards consideration, but the opening date kept continually getting pushed back. The most recent estimate is “late fall.”

Atlanta already knows the team behind Lucian can combine a fantastic wine list with thoughtful food and a carefully curated retail experience; they’ve started doing it again at Sargent, the combination bistro and bookstore that hadn’t yet opened when our scouts hit the city in early August. The classic menu and gorgeous space are already catching attention in the city; we’re also keeping our eyes on the upcoming opening of Thai-style bar Some Luck from the Talat Market team, slated to open any day now.

This new modern Mexican restaurant was only a few days old when our correspondent Matthew Kang stopped by in early September. Our LA team has high standards for tacos, and Kang says the top-notch Chihuahuan food here could already hold its own even when competing with standout California options. Kang appreciated Chiwas’s delicious seafood and short ribs, and approachable, homey vibe; we’ll be back to see how the restaurant matures.

October brought the debut of this ambitious restaurant from chef Jonathan Granada, and editor Dianne de Guzman is ready to try the tableside duck, laminated brioche, and a gougeres-like Parmesan tart — all set inside an Art Deco-style former post office.

We thought this long-in-the-works, highly anticipated Filipino cocktail bar might open in time for us to visit Detroit and check it out this year, but the project from Tyler Olivier and Marcee Sobredilla is still wrapping up construction.

This Evanston, Illinois, project is the first full-service restaurant from Chicago barbecue royalty D’Andre Carter and Heather Bublick. The restaurant is a true celebration of their community, decked out with local art and paired with a steakhouse-esque menu. It opened just outside our 2026 cutoff, and it’s looking like an exciting time for barbecue in the Windy City in general, as Chicago also awaits the opening of Sanders BBQ Prime in Hyde Park.

Lielle was a hit with the Eater LA team when it opened this year, and our team might even be more enamored with follow-up Marée, which just missed our window with its early September opening. At a recent visit, Matthew Kang noted the creamy mussels au gratin and Instagram-worthy squab, and says the au poivre burger earns its $42 price tag.

In the run-up to the COP31 U.N. climate change conference, scientists have revealed that global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to drop by 0.4% this year, driven by growth in installed wind and solar power capacity, as well as oil price hikes caused by the Iran conflict. But climate goals are still unlikely to be met.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The world's carbon emissions from oil, gas and coal are projected to decrease by 0.4% this year, driven partly by the expansion of solar and wind power capacity and the price increases caused by the Iran conflict, according to a new report.

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget report was published in the journal Earth System Science Data Nov. 10 and is due to be presented at the U.N. Climate Change Conference's COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, this week.

Global carbon emissions have increased steadily since record-keeping began. This year is projected to have a slight decrease in fossil-fuel emissions, but that is partly due to price increases caused by the Iran conflict.

It is the first time annual carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels have fallen since the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. But the overall emissions picture suggests the world is still likely to miss key climate goals.

"It is an encouraging sign that the growth of emissions is slowing and decarbonisation efforts are starting to make a difference," said Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London who wasn't involved in the research. "However, at 0.4%, the projected decline is very small," Rogelj told Live Science in an email.

The report projects 38.2 billion metric tons (42.1 billion U.S. tons) of emissions of the climate-warming greenhouse gas CO2 from fossil fuel sources this year. Greenhouse gases trap heat by absorbing the sun's radiation, and as their concentrations in the atmosphere increase, so do global average temperatures, leading to altered weather patterns and higher sea levels, as well as other major impacts.

The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand

Part of the 0.4% reduction in CO2 emissions is attributable to 40 countries that have cut emissions over the past decade while growing their economies. These include the U.S., Australia, New Zealand, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Japan and about 30 countries in the European Union, the researchers reported.

When it comes to some of the biggest emitters, annual CO2 emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9% in China, 1.3% in the U.S., 1.5% in the European Union and 1% in Japan, but India's annual CO2 emissions are projected to grow by 4.4%.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Carbon emissions are projected to decrease slightly in the U.S., China and the E.U. but to increase in India.

Fossil-fuel-linked CO2 emissions from the rest of the world are projected to decrease by 0.7%, driven mainly by a 1.9% drop in oil emissions. Some of the report authors suggested in an accompanying paper in Nature Climate Change that this is a short-term response to the global supply constraints and increased prices triggered by the Iran conflict.

"The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand," Rogelj said.

While fossil fuel emissions and demand for oil are declining globally, overall demand for energy is actually increasing.

"Based only on the demand for energy, which has grown, we would have expected an increase in fossil CO2 emissions by about 0.8 gigatonnes," said study co-author Judith Hauck, a biogeoscientist at the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research in Germany.

About two-thirds of that increase in demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, showing that clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions, Hauck said. However, the hike in energy prices that resulted from the Iran conflict also decreased demand by 0.4%, she said.

"So only together with the energy crisis did we bring the change in emissions down to negative," Hauck told Live Science, adding that she expects CO2 emissions to rebound if the conflict ends, as they did after the temporary emissions drop caused by the lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The exceptional circumstances that energy markets experienced this year make it clear that the small projected emissions decline is no reason to declare that emissions are now reducing, but there are hopeful signs, Rogelj said.

"Despite my muted enthusiasm about whether these lower emissions for 2026 represent the start of a long-term decline, the analysis shows encouraging signs of deeper long-term structural changes," he said. "But this shift must accelerate to ensure it is not outpaced by energy demand growth."

The report found that clean energy growth isn't yet fast enough to drive a steady decline in global CO2 emissions attributable to fossil fuels. The study authors expect that to happen in the next few years, Hauck said, as long as there is a continued push to deploy solar and wind power, batteries and electric vehicles.

CO2 emissions from fossil fuels are just part of the picture, though. Because of increases in human-caused peat fires, deforestation and forest fires linked to dry El Niño conditions, total global CO2 emissions from all sources this year are projected to increase slightly from 42.8 billion metric tons (47.2 billion U.S. tons) last year to reach a record 43.3 billion metric tons (47.7 billion U.S. tons) this year, according to the report.

This means that the total budget of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming reaches 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels is now just 150 billion metric tons (165 billion U.S. tons) ‪—‬ equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.

Hauck, like many climate scientists, thinks we have already missed our chance to hit the 1.5 C target and could only get back to that level through extensive removal of CO2 from the atmosphere.

"I'm still hopeful for something between 1.5 and 2 C [3.6 F]," Hauck said. "But for 1.5 degrees, we would need to see such a drastic strong drop in emissions. Based on what we've seen in the past years, even with this strong increase in avoided emissions, I don't think we can make that."

To halt global warming from increasing ever further, the world needs to be more ambitious in its planned emissions cuts, said Rogeli. We need to bring annual emissions down to zero to protect future generations from a double whammy of “having to try to transform economies so that they produce less climate pollution, while dealing with the impacts and damages of an increasingly adverse climate system," he said.

Editor's Note: This article was updated on Wednesday, Nov. 11 at 8:45 a.m. E.D.T. to note that the conclusions about the effect of the Iran conflict on fossil fuel emissions came from a Nature Climate Change paper written by some of the report authors.

Chris Simms is a freelance journalist who previously worked at New Scientist for more than 10 years, in roles including chief subeditor and assistant news editor. He was also a senior subeditor at Nature and has a degree in zoology from Queen Mary University of London. In recent years, he has written numerous articles for New Scientist and in 2018 was shortlisted for Best Newcomer at the Association of British Science Writers awards.

#6383. Tears of the Lion: Catching the 2026 Leonid Meteors

Why you should watch for the November Leonid meteors this year.

Itâs always worth being vigilant when skywatching in mid- to late November. Every year, a few Leonid meteors punctuate the November sky morning sky around the 17th. These silent harbingers are only a hint at the showerâs true storm potential, which culminates once every three decades.

The Leonid meteor shower can put on a true spectacle, and while 2026 isnât expected to be a âstorm year,â we could be due for some enhanced activity in the late 2020s going into the early 2030s.

The source of the Leonid meteor shower is periodic comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. On a 33 year orbit, comet 55P reaches perihelion 0.975 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun just inside Earthâs orbit once again on May 20, 2031.

Hubble captures Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Credit: NASA/HST/STScI

In 2026 the Moon phase is favorable at 41% illuminated, reaching 1st quarter phase a day after the showerâs peak night on November 16-17th. This means the Moon sets in the west, right as the radiant rises to the east.

The peak of the 2026 Leonids is set for November 17th at 3:00 Universal Time (UT), favoring Europe towards dawn, and North America just a few hours later. While 2026 is projected to be a 20 meteors per hour peak year, you just never know what a particular shower might have in store.

The Leonids are also real fast movers, approaching the Earth nearly head-on with a combined velocity of close to 70 kilometers per second. This is very near the theoretical maximum for inner solar system meteors. Most years only see a paltry 20 or so meteors per hour, though when the parent comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle is near perihelion, great storms are possible.

The Leonids hail from the backwards, question mark-shaped âSickle of Leoâ asterism. The radiant tracks from the +3rd magnitude star Epsilon Leonis past the bright double star Algieba in November. If you can trace a meteorâs flight back to this region, itâs a Leonid.

As an added treat in 2026, the planets Mars and Jupiter are very nearby, along with the bright star Regulus and the antihelion point towards which our planet is currently headed.

The rising Leonid radiant in 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

The Leonids top out with great outbursts every 33 years. A loose definition for a âmeteor stormâ is when the zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) tops out at about a 1,000 per hour, which is a fast-paced rate of one meteor every 3-4 seconds. Keep in mind, the ZHR is an extrapolated, ideal rate, assuming dark skies with the showerâs radiant directly overhead at the zenith. Most observers will always see less in reality, as fainter meteors slip by.

Records of the Leonids go all the way back to Arab annuals dating from 902 AD. 1833 saw an historic storm from the shower, as frightened residents along the U.S. Eastern Seaboard awoke to a sky awash in meteors. This single event was not only responsible in part for several religious movements of the day in the U.S., but also helped to push the modern scientific understanding of meteors from a purely atmospheric phenomenon to one originating from space.

A depiction of the Great Leonid Storm of 1833, depicted in 1889 by Adolf Vollmy. Credit: Public Domain.

The morning of November 17, 1966 saw a formidable performance from the shower, with observed rates over the southwestern U.S. topping out at an estimated 160,000 per hour (!)

I still remember catching the 1998 Leonids from the deserts of Kuwait, a year before the advertised outburst in 1999. The meteors lit up the desert floor just seconds apart towards sunrise with brilliant photo-flash flares. The spectacle continued right up until dawn. To date, it was still one of the best meteor showers Iâve ever witnessed.

Are we in for another great âmeteor stormâ in or around 2033? Well, we passed the mid-point in 2017. We did see a steady uptick in meteor activity through the late 1990s leading up to 1999. A caveat, however is in order with the approach of the Leonids in the early 2030s. Current models suggest we wonât see any great storms on the 2031 and 2064 passes of the comet, with 2099 being the next great âstorm yearâ. We may, however, still see respectable showers in excess of 100 per hour in the early 2030s laid down by older streams, topping the annual Perseid and Geminid meteors.

A Leonid double-shot. Credit: Eliot Herman

Observing a meteor shower is as simple as laying back and watching the sky, no special equipment needed. All you need is clear, dark skies and patience. Youâll see more in the early morning hours, as Earth hurdles headlong into the oncoming meteor stream. Imaging Leonids is a simple as setting up a tripod-mounted DSLR camera equipped with a wide-field lens to take long exposure shots of the sky, and seeing what turns up. An intervalometer hand control works great to automate this process.

An all-sky capture featuring a Leonid meteor. Credit: Eliot Herman.

Finally, be sure to count and record what you see, and send those observations to the International Meteor Organization.

Weâll see what the coming years has in store for the November Leonid meteors. One thing is for certain: youâll see zero meteors if you donât try. Time will tell if the coming years see the Leonids roar once again.

David Dickinson is a freelance science writer and long-time sky watcher. He has built telescopes and observatories, chased eclipses, and travels and observes with his wife, Myscha, on a mission to get âeyes on the skyâ worldwide. #6382. The 2026 Chefs of the Year

Five U.S. chefs making waves in their communities with compelling menus

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Each of the chefs featured in our new national Chef of the Year category made news in a major way. But their most recent projects are just one part of their story.

This year we celebrate five chefs who are making an impact both on the city where they cook and on the larger culinary conversation. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

San Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking.

In the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel, the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history.

Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican ingredients. The menu channels Laura’s upbringing in Guerrero and her family’s Sinaloan roots, as recounted through mariscos and maiz, moles and salsa macha. The ceviche Acapulqueño reimagines the Fanta- and ketchup-laden version instead with marigold flowers and preserved Seville oranges dressing tender shrimp and raw scallop; petals — and three fried shrimp heads — adorn the top. Duck enmoladas showcase the power of mole negro against a seasonal mole (sometimes a peach manchamanteles, other times a rhubarb rendition, but always compelling). Chochoyotes, a lesser-seen dish in San Francisco, demonstrates the restaurant’s ability to apply masa in different ways — in this case, dumplings — while harnessing the earthy flavor of huitlacoche. Maria Isabel is both a conduit for diners to connect with complex Mexican flavors and a view into Laura’s vision of the Mexico of her past and future. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

Chef Carlos Delgado’s meteoric rise in D.C. began in 2022 with the opening of tiny tasting room Causa, located in Shaw, where he sends diners on a seafaring voyage along the Peruvian coastline and into the Andes he grew up around, and its accompanying upstairs pisco destination Bar Amazonia. His meticulous sourcing and culinary skills quickly drew critical acclaim.

2026 might be the Lima native’s biggest year yet: His breakout project, Maru San, commanded instant Capitol Hill buzz upon opening in February for its orchestra of Nikkei-style hand rolls, sashimi, and other polished seafood plates he and fellow José Andrés alum Simon Lam pass across a 25-seat black marble counter under a big pink octopus mural, as his favorite tropical house blasts in the background. A rare few get to sample the restaurant’s elaborate tasting menu full of ingredients like high-end uni and dry-aged fish; reservations for the 15-course feast are nearly impossible to get.

The ambitious chef, at 36, isn’t afraid to stretch in many directions. He linked up with the Eaternity Group last year to give the Mediterranean-themed La Vie a needed menu makeover at D.C.’s Wharf development — meanwhile, at least one more Maru San is in the works elsewhere in D.C.

Sounds a lot like his former mentor: Before Causa, Delgado honed his craft under José Andrés as the longtime executive chef at Penn Quarter’s Peruvian mainstay China Chilcano. They still text frequently. — Tierney Plumb, Northeast editor

While Amir Hajimaleki has had American-leaning restaurants in Austin for well over a decade, he hasn’t had the opportunity to fully express himself as an Iranian-born, Texas-raised chef. That is until he opened Roya, his most personal restaurant and a project that has been in the works for more than eight years. Here, he manifests the depth and diversity of Persian cuisine, a bold feat for the middle of Texas. The space, designed with his brother Ali Hajimaleki, feels transportive with intricate tile mosaics, burnished gold and dark blue hues, and delicate chandeliers.

There’s been an electric energy to the Philly restaurant scene in recent years. The city, ever the underdog, has long punched above its weight; now, the rest of the world has come to the same realization. Amid this buzz, two newer restaurants have outrun the shadow cast by the city’s big names: Cambodian noodle house Mawn, which opened in 2023, and Southeast Asian oyster house and raw bar Sao, which opened last September.

At their helm is the slick, stylish Phila Lorn. The restaurants he runs with his wife Rachel feel singular, blending the influences of his Philadelphia upbringing with his Cambodian background in food that feels playfully free and emboldened by a lack of boundaries between cuisines. At Mawn, funnel cake meets coconut macaroons, and vinegar peppers enhance scallops in red curry. At Sao, the crispy rice in the nam khao salad, which features Italian sausage, feels analogous to arancini. Tuna carpaccio is served with crispy shallots and jalapeños, then cured in lime until it picks up the aura of the bowls of beef pho on Washington Avenue.

Hear Lorn talk, with his South Philly-bred bravado (and requisite uses of “jawn”) giving him a commanding presence, and it’s clear that the city’s culinary community is listening, rallying, and getting stoked to eat more of his food. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez had a vision that started in his small California city of El Centro, an agricultural city near the U.S.-Mexico border. There, he hatched a plan to create a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Trained at top kitchens in Los Angeles and beyond, Lopez researched by going deep into the desert, armed with a camera and his wits. A year later, he and his wife June Chee carried the project to Tucson, a larger venue still deeply embedded in the desert, but with a new audience.

Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. Barrel fruit (a yellow cactus) topped with the tang of pickled chiltepin leaves is the first bite, a luscious treat you may never see on a European plate. Quail breast arrives on a metal skewer dressed in pickled yucca, hovering over a jujube broth like a quiet offering. Goat roasted in agave, pit barbacoa-style, is unveiled tableside and served over softened tepary beans.

At every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. His message — seeing the value and beauty of this landscape, its people, its ingredients, and the way it all comes through the cooking — is the luscious pith of the cactus you find beneath the surface of the American Southwest. — Matthew Kang, correspondent

#6381. 5 Cozy Meals Our Editors Make With Boxed Stuffing

Each month in Well Stocked, our staff shares unfussy recipe ideas that you can call upon any day of the week. Because yes, our editors love to cook, but sometimes we need to get dinner on the table 12 minutes ago. That’s when we look to pantry and fridge staples that can quickly morph into delicious meals. This month, it’s all about boxed stuffing.

Few Thanksgiving dishes inspire as many strong opinions as stuffing slash dressing. In a baking dish or the bird itself? Sourdough or white bread? Fresh herbs or dried? Sausage or nah? There are the purists, who insist on drying their own bread, chopping aromatics, and seasoning everything from scratch. Then there are the Stove Top loyalists, who grew up on that unmistakable red box and remain fiercely faithful. Site director Rachel Tepper Paley is firmly in the latter camp. “My late father considered boxed Stove Top the Platonic ideal of stuffing, so I grew up with the uber-savory stuff on every Thanksgiving table,” she says. “We continue to serve it every year in his honor.”

And then there’s a particularly resourceful subset of boxed-stuffing devotees: the maximalists who see the box as a pantry staple, not just a holiday shortcut. Our editors happen to be among them. Read on for all the ways they’re thinking outside the box.

The first time I tried my colleague Jesse Szewczyk’s Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet in the Test Kitchen, I immediately started plotting all the occasions I could make it: Friendsgiving, a random Tuesday, football Sunday, date night. Its deliciousness caught me off guard. Jesse sears chicken thighs until golden and crisp, then uses the schmaltzy drippings (a.k.a liquid gold) to season the boxed stuffing. Dotted with sweet-tart cranberry gems, then baked with the chicken nestled back in, it’s basically Thanksgiving in one pan—and a recipe I plan to make well beyond November. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

When I find myself with instant stuffing, I like to make a baked eggs situation. I’ll make the stuffing according to the box’s directions in a shallow, oven-proof skillet. With the heat on (so the stuffing continues to crisp), I’ll toss in some greens like kale or spinach until they’re just barely wilted. Then, I’ll use a spatula to make a couple divots throughout and crack an egg into each. From there, I’ll pop the skillet into a 375°F oven and bake until the whites are set, about 15 minutes. A drizzle of green hot sauce and some salty feta crumble or sliced avocado, and I’m ready to eat. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

The way I see it, boxed stuffing mix is really close to a box of well-seasoned breadcrumbs. So why not use it as a savory panade that transforms lean ground turkey into tender meatballs? Senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk called this sheet-pan dinner Turkey and Stuffing Meatballs, but it honestly delivers all the flavors of Thanksgiving in one simple meal. You’ve got creamy baby Yukon gold potatoes and snappy green beans, plus a dipping sauce made from another autumn pantry staple, canned cranberry sauce, with lemon and honey to serve alongside. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

As a person who works in food media, I end up with my fair share of “what can I do with this?” ingredients. So while I firmly believe that no Thanksgiving dressing matters as much as my classic cornbread and biscuit version, I am no stranger to boxed stuffing. Frequently, it becomes a crust for baked fish. I’ve used Anna Stockwell’s easy no-recipe-required crispy fish method dozens of times since it first published, and it never disappoints. Best of all, you can use whatever bits and bobs you have lying around to build out the meal, and it’s relatively hands-off. Wins all around. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

For cozy season, there is nothing more comforting than carbs on carbs. I’ve always loved pasta with breadcrumbs (every which way), but leave it to senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk to make that classic combo even better: In this recipe, instead of using plain breadcrumbs or Italian seasoned ones, he swaps in stuffing mix blitzed in the food processor. Brilliant. It’s a highly flavorful topping for pasta with sausage and kale, a total delight for a cold night. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

#6380. A Universe Without Dark Matter? Radical New Model Challenges Modern Cosmology

An older universe could give unexpectedly mature early galaxies billions more years to grow, according to a model that also reproduces galaxy rotation without dark matter.

To explain how galaxies rotate, the standard model of the universe relies on dark matter, an unseen source of gravity. A new paper published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society reports that an alternative model can reproduce the rotation curves of all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database without dark matter. These curves show how orbital speeds change with distance from a galaxy’s center, giving researchers a way to test the gravity their model predicts.

The galaxy study is part of a series of tests conducted during 2025 and 2026 by Rajendra Gupta, an adjunct professor in the University of Ottawa’s Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras. They compared important astronomical observations with predictions from CCC+TL, a model that puts the universe’s age at 26.7 billion years and proposes that neither dark matter nor dark energy is needed.

The standard cosmological model is called ΛCDM, short for lambda cold dark matter. Lambda, written as the Greek letter Λ, represents the cosmological constant associated with dark energy, which accounts for the universe’s accelerating expansion. “Cold” means that the dark matter moves slowly compared with light. Scientists have searched for dark matter and dark energy for decades, but neither has been directly detected.

CCC+TL stands for “covarying coupling constants plus tired light.” It combines the idea that fundamental quantities governing forces and particle interactions evolve together over time with the proposal that light loses energy as it travels. Under this framework, changing fundamental constants could produce effects usually attributed to dark matter and dark energy.

Putting that proposal to the test required more than adjusting the settings in existing cosmology software. CCC+TL changes the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and the universe’s expansion. For each test, Gupta and Samaras developed equations and computer code consistent with their model.

Beyond individual galaxies, the researchers examined the Bullet Cluster. There, the extra gravitational effect predicted by CCC+TL tracks the galaxies rather than the hot, X-ray-emitting gas. The team describes this result as an early proof of concept that needs further study.

“Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants,” says Gupta, whose paper on the origin of dark matter and dark energy explores this idea.

An older universe would also change how astronomers interpret the large, mature galaxies they keep finding early in cosmic history. Those observations have raised questions for ΛCDM because galaxies need time to grow. How much time they had depends on the model used to interpret their redshift, a measure of how much their light has shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths.

For observations during cosmic dawn that correspond to a universe about 300 million years old under the standard model, CCC+TL gives an age of about 4.6 billion years at the same observed redshift. That leaves much more time for galaxies to develop. In calculations reported in Galaxies 13, 115, early galaxies come out about 12 times larger in size and mass than the standard model predicts.

“Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies,” Gupta explains. “We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached.”

The James Webb Space Telescope’s GLIMPSE program plans to search for galaxies at redshifts that may exceed 50, potentially providing a test of that prediction. At those redshifts, the standard model may leave too little time for massive galaxies to form. CCC+TL does not impose the same time constraint.

The researchers also tested whether their framework could account for evidence from much earlier in cosmic history. Its predictions for the amounts of hydrogen, helium, and other light elements formed shortly after the Big Bang matched those of the standard model. It also agreed with cosmic-chronometer measurements, which use galaxy ages to estimate how quickly the universe has expanded over time.

A separate study of time dilation in supernova observations also supports CCC+TL, although that paper remains under review. Time dilation here refers to the stretching of the observed timescale of a stellar explosion. The team’s work also extends to the cosmic microwave background, the radiation left over from the early universe.

“Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations,” Gupta says. “A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.”

“The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ΛCDM limits,” concludes Gupta.

Reference: “A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology” by Rajendra P. Gupta and Nikolaos Samaras, 25 June 2026, Universe. DOI: 10.3390/universe12070193

I’ve been challenging the standard model of gravity/spacetime in online video demonstrations from 2012 through 2025 (e.g., https://odysee.com/@charlesgshaver:d/5Gravity:c). In my model of gravity it’s induced by some still unidentified higher force to radiate in pulsing angular lines of attractive force and rotation intensifies its strength in all matter/objects. And, I’ve been challenging the accelerating expansion of the universe based upon expanding lines of gravity force accelerating (blueshift) photons as they are emitted by distant stars and decelerating (redshift) them as they arrive to earth. I agree that dark energy and dark matter are not necessary to explain the rotation of galaxies and that the age, and the size of the universe still need to be determined. My most recent gravity experiment, “Disproving Time Dilation,” is in a final stage of ‘double-checking’ the accuracy of my test timepiece, A paper and a new video are planned.

and all of this has been debunked utterly

Since there are no papers that are published in peer review (or even a prominent physicist publishing with that name), there is no challenge – it is online spam.

Hitchens razor is the spam filter here: “What can be asserted without evidence can also be dismissed without evidence.”

Professor Larsson, I’ve been thinking of writing you to explain my delays since beginning in March, evolving experiment design issues and unanticipated mechanical failures, but I’m so close to competition now. And, as I stated previously, I have no peers. I have four low budget video demonstrations that curious scientists could replicate but there doesn’t seem to be any anymore. ‘Shaver’s Razor’ is the reality check here: “Artificial experiments tend to result in artificial findings.” I have a rough draft paper in the works.

Well, the CCC+TL model seems to be a very promising way to eliminate Dark Matter and Dark Energy from our universe. I will be looking for more developments from testing this models claims.

That will be an infinite looking time, since it fails out of the gate. All astronomical objects agree, independently of cosmology, that the matter universe is no more than 14 billion years old. And standard cosmology agrees perfectly with that!

We regularly see articles challenging the existence of dark matter/energy, which many scientists have built their careers on .

What we need is a cage match, where one persuasion or the other wins.

Science sites presenting peer review published material in a neutral way is not the problem.

The cage fight is in professional publications and conferences. There may be a humorous but “dark universe” (unseen) side ruckus if professional physicists becomes fed up with spammers that may attempt to send them email. They may cross post their unasked for material and ask them to fight it out. Ethics aside, it would be funny if it happens. (It looks like a conspiracy theory – which would easily trigger more spam since conspiracy theory essentially is what some of these notionally ‘alternative’ theories are – but IIRC there is this old anecdote that described something like that in the before-web-times.)

Ah yes, since we are into “spam physics” territory thanks to some comments: I notices that besides the current SpaceX mission that I watch in another window consistently doing trackable gravitationally guided orbits rejecting “flat Earth” notions it does something else. The spacecraft is sufficiently long that you can estimate the fish lens camera distortions (and of course there are proper ground photos showing straight cylinder shape). So independently of Earth observations you can estimate that effect and deduct it from the rotating Earth horizon *by eye*, effortlessly rejecting some common ‘physics’ spam.

I dunno what “no dark matter” spammers makes of neutrino experiments, since morally neutrino’s mass is 0.2 % of dark matter, just not the dominant massive (cold) dark matter we observe with other means.

This is why modifications to general relativity – especially Gupta’s old hobby horse – fails: They predict one thing well (usually rotation curves) but fail to give the correct upper limit on age that we get from stars, or as here size of galaxies which is observed by other means than rotation curves.

Props if they also get a second right (primordial nucleosynthesis, where total baryon density figures in). But dark matter alone has *tens of independent* observation types agreeing on its existence (Wikipedia), and LCDM has no rival as of yet.

I was going to leave it there but then I thought that it would be obvious that they somehow tried to duck the age question so I needed to do due diligence on that. But when I looked for a reference I noted that the article text implies that they may have not and I can stand by my assessment until someone proves me wrong. But more importantly, the article describe their model as a “tired light” model, which was rejected over a century ago on the grounds that images then would be more fuzzy. (And with today’s technology it should be even worse.)

Wikipedia: “Tired light is a class of hypothetical redshift mechanisms that was proposed as an alternative explanation for the redshift-distance relationship. These models have been proposed as alternatives to the models that involve the expansion of the universe. The concept was first proposed in 1929 by Fritz Zwicky, who suggested that if photons lost energy over time through collisions with other particles in a regular way, the more distant objects would appear redder than more nearby ones.

Zwicky acknowledged that any sort of scattering of light would blur the images of distant objects more than what is seen. Additionally, the surface brightness of galaxies evolving with time, time dilation of cosmological sources, and a thermal spectrum of the cosmic microwave background have been observed—these effects should not be present if the cosmological redshift was due to any tired light scattering mechanism.[1][2][3] Despite periodic re-examination of the concept, tired light has not been supported by observational tests and remains a fringe topic in astrophysics.[4]”

#6379. Shape-Shifting Robotic "Slugs" Could One Day Crawl Across Alien Worlds

Robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts. But they normally have wheels. Or in some cases, rotors. While those solutions are great on flat ground, they struggle with jagged boulders or tight crevices. So engineers have been working on alternative robotic form factors, and a recent paper in Nature Machine Intelligence from researchers at Colorado State Universityâs Adaptive Robotics Lab, describes a unique morphology using a design principle typically seen in architecture rather than robotics - tensegrity.

Tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century. Itâs a blend of the words âtensionâ and âintegrityâ, and at its core it uses rigid rods that push outwards against elastic cables that pull inwards. So, instead of relying on heavy metal hinges, the rods âfloatâ on a web of tension.

This isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though. NASA has been exploring its use cases for over a decade, perhaps most notably with the SUPERball - a spherical cage designed to withstand high-speed planetary landings without parachutes by absorbing the shocks of impact across its network of cables.

Fraser talks about some other robots that could end up exploring other worlds.

But this is one of the first times the idea has been applied to robotics. The CSU researchers have developed what they call the Tensegrity-based Continuum Robot (TeCoBot). Measuring in at around 587 mm (~2 ft) long and weighing around 600 grams, the cylindrical bot combined a squishy, flexible spine with adaptable dual mechanical claws, which provide the real interesting use cases of the technology.

TeCoBotâs body is made out of four stacked icosahedral tensegrity modules that create a continuous, flexible backbone. Each module is built around six lightweight rods suspended inside a 3D printed stretchy lattice. Three cables made up of 40-lb braided fishing wire run through the center of the robot, and by pulling on each of them with small motors attached to its base, the robot can bend in any direction - like an âelephantâs trunkâ as a press release puts it. It can also scrunch down to around half its original size if all three lines are pulled at the same time.

But whatâs most interesting about the technology is its modularity, which relies on the claws on either end. These claws are swappable, so if a robot needs to handle delicate cargo engineers can put a soft-padded claw on it. But, if needed, those soft pads can be swapped out for a heavier duty gripper claw that uses a worm gear to clamp and hold onto another gripper without draining any battery.

Fraser talks about the concept of "grey goo" - or self-replicating robots able to automate space exploration.

This unlocks all sorts of additional opportunities. As a stand-alone single robot, TeCoBot is already relatively capable - it can inch along like a caterpillar, roll sideways, and even climb vertically. It also exhibits what roboticists call âembodied intelligenceâ that means its body can naturally give way when bumped or when it runs into something without needing a whole control system to adjust to the changed environment.

But when they combine together, they unlock whole new operating modes. Using their claws to grab one another, three TeCoBots can self-configure into a wide variety of shapes. The paper discusses three robots wrapping themselves around a large pipe, and forming a H-shaped walker to crawl through tight spaces. But perhaps most interestingly for anyone who hates cleaning as much as this author, they are also capable of teaming up to clean off a table.

Those feats might not seem immediately applicable to space exploration, but the underlying modularity and adaptability would be extremely useful in the rough craters of the Moon or underground caverns on Mars. Weâve already reported on a snake robot designed to explore those exact locations, and this seems like a step up in functionality from that.

Video of the TeCoBot in action. Credit - Adaptive Robotics Lab YouTube Channel

That being said, it still has a long way to go before weâd see it on another heavenly body. Currently, engineers have to manually control the bots via a WiFi connection - which isnât exactly easy on deep space missions. But they do plan to make improvements on the design, upgrading the motors for faster movement and adding swarm intelligence to allow dozens of these modular robots to band together. If that development goes as planned, these elephant trunk styled robots might serve as some of our most intrepid deep space explorers.
