In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6344. The 9 Best Gaming Keyboards for Next-Level Play

Get speedy response times, greater accuracy, and advanced customization options.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

As much as we’d like to believe the old adage about a carpenter and their tools, better equipment is a necessity if you want to take your gameplay to the next level. Just as a great gaming mouse ensures rocksteady aim, a proper gaming keyboard has quick, responsive keys to execute your movements precisely.

From strafing to crouching to placing items, not just any old keyboard will do. Dedicated gaming keyboards offer more comfort, precise control, and added functionality over our favorite ergonomic keyboards, making it easy to streamline abilities in MMOs, dodge bullets in online shooters, or move players around in strategy games.

The keyboards we recommend are highly rated by both reviewers and consumers, delivering top gaming performance with responsive touch and high customizability so you can dial in the perfect profile for each game.

For more great keyboards, check out our picks for the best gaming speakers, best gaming monitors, best gaming chairs, and best gaming desktops.

As Popular Mechanics’ resident consumer tech expert and a lifetime gaming enthusiast, I’ve tested some of the most popular gaming keyboards over the years. I prefer the snappiness of mechanical switches, but I’ve come around to membrane options for their quiet and fast keys.

This article reflects my own list of the best gaming keyboards that I created to narrow down my next keyboard purchase. Beyond our consumer tech experts' personal experience, we also researched reliable sources such as TechRadar, PC Mag, and PC Gamer, and read consumer reviews to select the top gaming keyboards. We’ve included a range of options to meet different budgets and preferences so you can find the one that’s right for you.

The Apex Pro has long led the pack thanks to its tunable actuation, and the third generation goes further. Its OmniPoint 3.0 magnetic switches give you 40 actuation levels per key, from a hair-trigger 0.1 mm to a deliberate 4.0 mm. You can set it shallow for fast play or deeper to cut down on typos.

The Gen 3 also adds three competitive features. Rapid Trigger resets a key the moment you let go. Rapid Tap snaps to your most recent key press so you can strafe and dodge faster. Protection Mode reduces accidental presses of neighboring keys. SteelSeries' QuickSet presets load pro-level settings automatically when your game launches, and the OLED screen lets you change actuation and profiles on the fly without opening software.

The tenkeyless layout leaves more room for your mouse. Quantum 2.0 Dual Wireless connects over lag-free 2.4GHz for gaming or Bluetooth for your other devices. Some owners say the battery life is only middling, and at about $300 it's a real investment. Still, few keyboards can match its speed and customization.

For an entry-level mechanical keyboard that won't break the bank, the Logitech G413 SE is a great pick. You won't get all the bells and whistles of more expensive models, but its tactile mechanical switches give each keystroke a satisfying bump. Six-key rollover anti-ghosting means even your most frantic key combinations register.

The SE also upgrades to PBT keycaps, which resist heat, wear, and the shiny fade that cheaper keycaps develop over time. Twelve function keys handle volume, play/pause, track skipping, lighting, and Windows lock. A brushed aluminum-magnesium alloy top case keeps flex to a minimum and gives the board a sleek look. If you'd rather have more desk space, Logitech also makes a tenkeyless version, the G413 TKL SE.

The G915 X TKL takes everything we loved about the original G915 TKL and refines it. At just 0.9 inches tall, it's one of the slimmest mechanical gaming keyboards around. Its brushed aluminum alloy plate also keeps flex to a minimum, so it's tougher than its size suggests.

Lightspeed wireless delivers lag-free play, and Bluetooth and wired modes let you switch between your gaming rig and your other devices. The tenkeyless layout drops the number pad, so your mouse has more room, while dedicated media and volume controls stay within reach. If you're heading to a tournament or just moving your setup to another room, the G915 X TKL is still the portable powerhouse to beat.

The ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless gives you nearly everything a full-size keyboard does, number pad included, in a body only about 1 cm wider than a typical 80 percent board. That leaves you more room for your mouse without giving up the keys you use for work.

Low-latency 2.4GHz wireless keeps gameplay lag-free. Bluetooth lets you pair up to three other devices, and you can plug in over USB-C when you need to. Battery life is the standout, with Asus rating it at up to 1,500 hours with the lighting off and about 90 hours with RGB on.

An aluminum alloy top plate, sound-dampening foam, and double-shot PBT keycaps give it a solid, refined feel. The hot-swappable board lets you swap in different switches whenever you want. A multifunction key and clickable roller handle volume, media, and lighting, and a padded magnetic wrist rest comes in the box for marathon sessions.

If you play MMOs or want shortcuts for streaming and editing, the BlackWidow V4 Pro has more programmable controls than almost any keyboard around. It has five dedicated macro keys down the left side, three more macro buttons along the edge of the chassis, and a multifunction Command Dial that can hold up to 100 custom modes. Razer's HyperShift adds a second layer to nearly every key, and the keyboard can save up to five profiles.

It's no slouch in-game, either. Full N-key rollover means every key registers even when you're mashing several at once, and an 8,000 Hz polling rate helps cut input delay. You can choose loud, satisfying Razer Green clicky switches or smooth Razer Yellow linear switches. Machined metal media keys and a volume roller sit in the top right corner, and an aluminum alloy top plate keeps the board sturdy.

The padded leatherette wrist rest snaps on magnetically and extends the keyboard's underglow, so the whole setup glows as one. It's big, so make sure you have the desk space, but if you want every command a single keypress away, the BlackWidow V4 Pro is the one to get.

If desk space is tight, or you want as much room as possible for your mouse, a 60 percent keyboard is the way to go. The Huntsman V3 Pro Mini trims the keyboard to the essentials without sacrificing features. Its analog optical switches let you set how far each key travels before it registers, so you can set it to shallow for hair-trigger movement or deeper to avoid accidental presses.

Rapid Trigger resets each key the moment you start to let go, so you can repeat inputs faster. Snap Tap prioritizes whichever direction you pressed most recently, making strafing quicker in shooters. The keyboard also has dual-purpose modifier keys that let one key do two jobs, which helps make up for the missing keys. Doubleshot PBT keycaps resist the shine that cheaper keycaps get over time.

The trade-off is that arrow keys, F-keys, and the number pad all move to a secondary layer, so expect a short adjustment period. For competitive players who want a small, fast keyboard, it's an excellent pick.

If you grew up with an original Xbox, this keyboard will feel instantly familiar. Its design is based on the console's Transparent Green Edition. RGB lighting glows through the jade-like translucent shell and double-layered keycaps, and the arrow keys are made of crystal-clear plastic. Taller, retro-style keycaps and a top-mount design finish the throwback look. It's officially licensed by Xbox, and the dedicated Xbox button opens the Windows Game Bar.

It also comes with 8BitDo's Dual Super Buttons, a pair of giant arcade-style buttons that plug into the keyboard. You can map them to a macro or any key without installing software, and up to four sets can connect at once. An aluminum plate keeps the 87-key layout sturdy, and the hot-swappable board lets you swap out the Kailh Jellyfish X switches later. A control panel at the top handles volume, connection mode, and button mapping with a simple turn and click.

It connects over 2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth 5.0, or USB. The 4,000 mAh battery lasts up to 280 hours over 2.4GHz and 300 hours over Bluetooth. Despite the branding, it works only with Windows PCs and Android devices, not Xbox consoles. If you want a PC keyboard that stands out in your setup, though, it's hard to beat.

Most keyboards will plug into a console, but they won’t always work. HyperX lists the Alloy Origins 65 as compatible with PlayStation 5, PlayStation 4, Xbox Series X|S, and Xbox One. It's a wired keyboard, so there's no Bluetooth pairing or wireless receiver to troubleshoot.

The 65 percent layout is small enough to sit on your lap, but it keeps dedicated arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home, and Delete for moving through menus and stores. The full aluminum body is sturdy, and the double-shot PBT keycaps have secondary functions printed on their sides, so the shortcuts are easy to find.

HyperX's switches come in linear Red or tactile Aqua, are rated for 80 million keypresses, and actuate at 1.8 mm. N-key rollover registers every keypress, and per-key RGB lighting shines through the exposed switches. The NGENUITY software only runs on PC, so set up your macros and lighting there, then save them to one of the keyboard's three onboard profiles.

Most gaming keyboards clack loudly enough to bother everyone in the room. The K65 Plus Wireless is much quieter, with Corsair putting a layer of foam and a silicone pad inside the case to absorb vibration. Combined with factory-lubed MLX Red linear switches, that turns each keystroke into a low, muted thock instead of a sharp clack. It's quiet enough for late-night sessions in a shared apartment or for typing during voice calls without your coworkers hearing every key.

The switches are light and smooth, and the hot-swappable board lets you swap in silent switches if you want to make it even quieter. The 75 percent layout keeps dedicated arrow keys and a function row in a compact frame, and a knurled metal knob in the corner can be programmed for volume or other controls.

Connect over 2.4GHz wireless for gaming, Bluetooth for a work laptop, or USB-C for charging. Battery life reaches up to 266 hours with the lighting off. The plastic case and plain keycaps give it a less premium feel, and the RGB lighting doesn't shine through the legends. Still, if you want a quieter keyboard without giving up gaming performance, it's an excellent choice.

Short of building a mechanical keyboard with your own layout design and keycaps, purchasing a factory gaming keyboard gives you plenty of advanced customization options.

Beyond aesthetic choices like lighting, you can program key bindings to perform menu shortcuts with a single press. These streamlined commands help you better focus on the in-game action.

Outside of gaming, macro keys (programmable keys) can help you create productivity shortcuts in all your programs. If you often use video editing software to edit gameplay clips, you can assign actions to macro buttons to create content faster. This is especially handy if you plan to use your gaming keyboard for everyday tasks, too.

Beyond individual key settings, some gaming keyboards include keyboard profiles with specific key functions and lighting tailored to each game you play. For example, a Cyberpunk-themed profile might set your keyboard to a neon yellow glow with the Q button bound to a quick attack.

Most first-person shooters map the Q button to a special ability or cover, but with individualized profile bindings, you can program each button to do what you want. Some titles, such as Diablo III, can even use your keyboard’s RGB lighting to indicate when you cast a spell or when your character is low on health, increasing immersion.

With tons of keys and lighting options, your keyboard’s body size determines just how many extra buttons or light sections can fit.

Bigger, longer, and uncut, full-sized keyboards include every single key you'll see on a typical keyboard (and more) for access to extra action buttons, a number pad, and dedicated media keys. There's more room to spread out, but full keyboards are less portable—well worth the compromise if you'll use your keyboard to type for work or if you need plenty of command keys for RTS or MOBAs.

Tenkeyless boards axe the right-hand number pad for a tighter shape. The result is a compact keyboard (at least 20 percent smaller than a full-size model) that’s easy to move and leaves you with more space on your desk to operate your mouse. If you don’t have to work with data entry and don't mind losing extra inputs, a tenkeyless board transports with ease and offers an organic typing experience.

Ditching the number pad and F-keys, compact keyboards are limited to the alphanumeric zone. They’re still capable of comfortable typing, but if you often use F commands, you’ll have to assign a number key to use with the function key. Once you have your compact keyboard configured, it’s by far the easiest keyboard to wield, albeit with extra steps for pulling up shortcuts.

Streamlined for command efficiency, one-handed keyboards trim the fat of all characters on the right half of your keyboard. With dead keys gone and game inputs in reach of your left hand, you have more precision than any other keyboard type. You’re still going to need a daily keyboard, however, as this style is meant to supplement your main keyboard, not replace it.

Mechanical keyboards use three switch types for feedback: tactile (usually brown), clicky (usually blue), and linear (usually red).

Tactile switches provide a small bump and subdued clack to confirm registered keystrokes. They are the most popular because they offer the feedback of clicky switches with speed similar to linear switches.

Clicky switches have a higher actuation pressure requirement to reduce typos while writing, a big bump for validation, and a signature loud click that’s music to any typist’s ears but a bane to coworkers’ and housemates’.

Linear speed switches are great for gaming because they’re smooth, offer minimal resistance, and have none of the noise of a brown or blue switch. People often bottom out on these red or silver keys since there’s no clear indication you’ve triggered their actuation point. Linear keys fire off on all cylinders, but they’re not so great for typing because their zippiness can cause typos.

Membrane keys aren’t mechanical and rely on a single mechanism under the keys to register presses. Some people complain that membrane inputs feel mushy, but they last longer than mechanical keys and cost much less because they don’t have an intricate system of moving parts.

It can be tempting to go for a cheap gaming keyboard and save the extra cash for a better gaming PC or monitor, but higher-quality mechanical switches—along with more durable materials like aluminum—can improve performance, provide a sturdier base, and increase reaction speed.

#6343. A 6-Million-Year-Old Whale Had a Face So Strange Scientists Thought It Was Crushed

A newly identified prehistoric whale had unusual adaptations that may have allowed it to hunt along the seafloor millions of years ago.

An ancient whale that lived millions of years ago had a skull so dramatically distorted that its face appeared pushed to one side. Its bony nostrils were displaced entirely to the left, and its oversized snout curved sharply downward. Scientists have identified the animal as Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale with the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a cetacean.

The fossil dates to the Late Miocene, approximately 6.3 to 5.6 million years ago, and belonged to a whale measuring about 2.7 meters (8.9 feet) long. Researchers believe its skull may also represent the greatest facial asymmetry known in any mammal.

Most vertebrates have skulls that are approximately symmetrical, with corresponding structures on either side of the head. Toothed whales are an exception. Their skulls have evolved asymmetrical shapes to accommodate specialized organs involved in producing sound and echolocation, allowing them to navigate and detect prey underwater.

“Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked,” explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study. He investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich and is now an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

The whale’s unusual anatomy suggests a feeding strategy very different from that of modern sperm whales, which pursue squid in deep ocean waters. Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have been adapted for searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal seas. Its thick, tubular snout contained dense bone and hardened cartilage that added weight toward the front of its body. The snout angled downward by 31 degrees, while reconstructions of the joint between the skull and first neck vertebra suggest the animal could lower its head by as much as 55 degrees.

“The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom,” explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, study co-author and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich. “The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.”

Unlike some modern marine mammals that forage along the bottom, Scaphokogia lacked specialized facial whiskers and visual adaptations associated with locating prey in sediment. Researchers therefore suspect it relied on its unusually developed biosonar system to detect food hidden in soft seabed deposits. This remains a hypothesis based on its anatomy rather than direct evidence of its hunting behavior. Its specialized ecological niche apparently disappeared as ocean conditions changed near the end of the Miocene.

The skull was recovered in the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru, a desert region famous for exceptionally preserved marine fossils. Benites-Palomino encountered the specimen in 2015 while working on his bachelor’s thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its extreme shape initially raised the possibility that geological forces had distorted the skull after the animal died.

“The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy – that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years,” says Benites-Palomino. “But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.”

The researchers chose a species name that reflects the animal’s unconventional appearance. Huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and describes something extravagant, flashy, bizarre, or aesthetically excessive.

“In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant, or difficult to categorize aesthetically,” says Benites-Palomino.

“When we looked at the proportions of this whale – with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout – it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.”

Reference: “Extreme cranial asymmetry in extinct benthic feeding sperm whales” by Aldo Benites-Palomino, Marcelo R. Sánchez-Villagra, Florencia Paolucci, Jorge Vélez-Juarbe, Alberto Collareta, Apolline Alfsen, Alton Dooley, Dan Omura, Mario Urbina, Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi and Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, 9 November 2026, Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11074-2

#6340. Scientists Discover Mysterious New Fish in the Red Sea – and Have Never Seen It Again

Scientists discovered a tiny new fish species in the Red Sea but have never found it again, suggesting it may live mostly on deeper reefs that remain largely unexplored.

In Greek mythology, Charon ferried the dead across a river into the underworld. People were traditionally buried with a coin to pay for the crossing. That tradition helped inspire the name of a newly described fish species from the northern Red Sea, Charon’s pygmygoby (Trimma charon).

“One of the most striking features of the new species is the golden spots scattered across its tail fin,” said study leader Viktor Nunes Peinemann of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) in Saudi Arabia. “They cover most of the fin and resemble small gold coins.”

The tiny fish is translucent, with a broad orange-red stripe and an unusual four-part eye. The two known specimens measure just 12 and 17 millimeters long, roughly half an inch and two-thirds of an inch.

The new species resembles the pallid pygmygoby (Trimma anaima), a fish found from East Africa to the Pacific but never recorded in the Red Sea. Genetic data suggest the two are close relatives, although further work is needed to confirm that relationship.

“While one species seems to have spread across much of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, its closest relative appears to have stayed in the Red Sea and evolved separately for millions of years,” said Peinemann.

Researchers collected the two specimens in May 2023 at Walih Island, at the entrance to a cave on a steep reef slope. They were found 30 meters, about 98 feet, below the surface, the maximum depth of the team’s scientific diving. Extensive searches of similar habitats since then have produced no further sightings. “So far, the entire species is known from only a single encounter and two specimens,” said Peinemann.

The team suspects that the encounter took place at the shallow edge of the species’ range. The fish may be more common on largely unexplored mesophotic reefs below 30 meters, where sunlight is faint. That possible habitat provides another connection to its mythological namesake.

“These dark, deeper, unexplored reefs could be viewed as a kind of ‘underworld’ beneath the shallow, well-lit, and better studied reefs most of us are more familiar with,” he said.

“Red Sea reefs below that depth almost certainly hold more undiscovered gobies.”

The discovery brings the number of known Trimma species in the Red Sea to 11, making it the region’s most species-rich goby genus. At least nine appear to live nowhere else in the world. To help researchers distinguish them, the paper provides an illustrated identification key to all 11 species, along with photographs and field notes describing where each lives.

The study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys. Peinemann is based in the Marine Science Program within KAUST’s Division of Biological and Environmental Science and Engineering. His co-authors are Matthew D. Tietbohl Talas and Michael L. Berumen of KAUST, and Sergey V. Bogorodsky of the Senckenberg Research Institute and Natural History Museum Frankfurt, Germany.

“Knowing which species are present, how to accurately identify them, and where they live, is the most foundational step to building a stronger understanding of these species and ecosystems,” said Peinemann. “They still have many secrets and deserve much more attention.”

Reference: “Trimma charon, a new species of pygmygoby (Teleostei, Gobiidae) from the Red Sea with a key to the Red Sea species of the genus” by Viktor N. Peinemann, Sergey V. Bogorodsky, Matthew D. Tietbohl Talas and Michael L. Berumen, 24 September 2026, ZooKeys. DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1293.204097

#6338. The 7 Best Car Battery Chargers for Roadside Emergencies

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Maintain your car battery—or bring a dead one back to life.

The 12-volt battery is one of the least complex components in modern vehicles but one of the most crucial. If it’s not in good condition, the engine won’t start, and none of the vehicle’s fancy systems will work. Car batteries have a limited lifecycle and deteriorate with time. This can happen for many reasons, including extended inactivity, extreme temperatures, or even something as simple as accidentally leaving the lights on after you turn off the engine.

That’s why it’s handy to have an external car battery charger so your engine is ready to go when you need it. A charger can also help extend your battery's life, for instance, in a vehicle you don't drive often—a weekend getaway camper or an old classic cruiser. Some chargers also have a jumpstart feature, eliminating the need for jumper cables (and the inconvenience of a required second vehicle).

You might be surprised to hear that electric vehicles use the same 12-volt car batteries as their internal combustion counterparts. Regardless, modern vehicles rely on this ancillary battery to power lights and onboard electronics when the ignition is off. Here, we’ve compiled the best chargers for cars and motorcycles, including everything from a solar-powered charger to a model that can revive several vehicles at once.

Noco’s Genius 10, the brand’s flagship single-vehicle charger, offers many cool features, including the ability to “force charge” a battery so dead it won't generate any voltage when you hook it up. (Most modern chargers won’t do this.) Maintenance and “desulfation” modes extend your battery's useful life while keeping it ready to go.

Unlike smaller, less ambitious chargers, the Genius 10 charges a vehicle battery to full power in the shortest safe time. It can even charge the new generation of lithium-ion car batteries, like the complex, expensive units fitted to many newer BMWs.

All the basic features are here at a very low price, including protection from reverse clamping and a “float mode” for fully charged batteries.

The included set of bolt-on leads lets you quickly connect and disconnect the charger. Operation couldn’t be simpler: a green light shows the Motopower is on, and a red light indicates charging status. With 1.5 amps of power, it charges slightly faster than most competitors in the low-price bracket.

Think of this 15-amp charger as a miniature version of the shop-grade Schumacher. It’s also the form and function that will be most familiar to older or experienced users. The included clamps are high-quality and should fit most cars. Just clamp on, plug in, and select one of three modes.

The 15-amp rapid charge is slightly more than the competition can manage, and a carrying handle makes it easy to place where you want it.

This charger is compact, light, easy to operate, and almost bombproof. It delivers a 3-amp charge, then automatically switches to float mode to maintain proper voltage and prevent overcharging.

A two-color LED indicates charging status, and if the battery voltage drops below a certain level, it resumes full charging output in adaptive mode. It’s compatible with most automotive batteries and can switch between 6- and 12-volt batteries with the push of a button. Its battery clamps are spark-proof, and the Battery Tender 3-Amp will automatically detect reverse polarity. It comes with a 5-year warranty and lifetime customer service.

Dealerships and race shops that used to scatter CTEK individual chargers throughout the building are now switching to the multi-vehicle Noco 2x4 model. It weighs just under 8 pounds, mounts to a wall, and can handle four vehicles at the same time, each in a different mode.

Want to float charge one car, recondition another, and bring two other dead batteries back to life in force-charge mode? Not a problem.

If you own a vehicle you only drive occasionally, an under-the-hood charger saves the hassle of disconnecting it from the battery and storing it each time you want to go for a cruise.

The compact Schumacher SC1300 mounts under the hood to supply up to 1.5 amps, while a built-in microprocessor automatically adjusts the charging rate to maintain an ideal charge state. Float mode delivers a small current when needed.

Reverse hook-up protection prevents the charger from working if the battery clamps are installed in reverse polarity, and the Schumacher automatically detects 6-volt or 12-volt batteries.

If an electrical outlet isn’t available or if you just want to use the sun to keep your battery topped off, the Sun Energize solar-powered charger is a reliable option. It trickle-charges a variety of automotive batteries, as well as some lithium batteries.

A built-in charge controller prevents overcharging; charging stops when a battery is topped off and automatically resumes when it drains.

An LED indicator shows charge and battery conditions. The 20.1 x 13.8 x 0.7-inch solar panel is larger than the other chargers here, but it’s built to handle high winds and heavy loads and is IP65 waterproof.

We tested some external battery chargers under varying weather conditions, while others were chosen based on feedback from car enthusiast friends. The selections represent a wide variety of chargers with different capabilities to match a broad range of use cases. We have years of experience traveling the country with these chargers and know their performance very well.

If you store a vehicle for long periods, you’ll want a charger to keep the battery from fully dying and turning into a paperweight. (It’s also nice to know it will start without jumper cables.) But a battery charger can make a difference in plenty of other situations.

If you regularly experience below-freezing temperatures at night, a charger with a maintenance function can significantly extend your battery's life. If you rarely drive more than a few miles at a time, a charger can prevent your battery from discharging too far—leaving you with a no-start condition. Last but not least, older vehicles often struggle to recharge slightly depleted batteries on the move, so starting the day with a fully charged battery can also extend the life of your alternator and charging system.

Charging power is traditionally measured in amps. Think of amps as the amount of juice that can be put back into the battery at any given time; for example, a 10-amp charger puts twice as much charge into the battery as a 5-amp one. A quick stroll through a listing of battery chargers can be confounding, though. Some have 40 amps, and some have 0.75 amps, and yet they do the same thing. In reality, the difference is easy to understand. The more power a charger has, the more quickly it can bring a dead battery back to life. The tradeoff is cost, size, and weight.

If you’re charging a small motorcycle battery or maintaining a good-condition battery in a cherished collector car, then a 0.75-amp charger will do just fine. If you’re worried that your pickup won’t start in the winter, 2 to 10 amps is a better bet. Any capability above that is mostly for mechanics who need to quickly charge or recondition batteries in the shop.

Every charger here can “maintain” a charged battery, keeping it from slowly discharging between uses. Most chargers can also bring a depleted battery back up to full power. A few chargers offer specialized modes like “desulfation,” which helps a battery regain its chemical balance through carefully timed charge-and-discharge cycles. A “quick charge” can very rapidly (but safely) prepare a battery for use. A few battery chargers also offer a “jump start mode” that can start a car or motorcycle with a dead battery, but this is rare, and most of the time you’ll need a separate jump starter for that task.

Most chargers in this roundup are designed for conventional lead-acid (flooded cell) or Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) batteries, which you’ll find in newer vehicles. If you have a vehicle with a lithium-ion battery, like some new BMWs, or a customized car with ultra-compact batteries from manufacturers like Braille, you’ll need a charger with that capability—different battery chemistries require specific charging protocols.

If you are dealing with a cramped garage, or travel between storage spaces throughout the seasons, consider a “wall wart” or direct-mount charger. The former keeps all the charging mechanisms in a large plug that some people might compare to model-train transformer plugs. The latter bolts into your car and plugs directly into the wall.

Not anymore. Today's smart chargers, like the ones in our article, won't overcharge a battery or give it more than it can handle. And choosing a more powerful charger won't shorten your battery's lifespan; quite the opposite, in fact!

Then you can coil the quick-disconnect cord in a convenient place, like inside a motorcycle fairing or under a car hood. The cables can melt when exposed to serious heat, so don't let them touch an exhaust pipe.

#6337. Scientists Crack a Decades-Old Mystery That Could Unlock Faster Internet

By untangling how the crystal barium titanate interacts with light, researchers have supplied data that could reduce costly trial and error in designing faster optical communication devices.

When light carries data through a communication device, absorption by the materials inside can weaken the signal. Engineers trying to build faster, more efficient devices need to predict how light will travel through those materials and how much will be lost before they commit to a design.

For a promising material called barium titanate, or BTO, those measurements have varied widely for decades. A KAIST-led research team has now clarified how it interacts with light, providing data that could help engineers design devices more reliably and reduce costly rounds of fabrication and redesign.

BTO offers a useful way to control light because applying an electric field changes its refractive index, a measure of how much light slows as it passes through a material. Its strong response to an electric field, known as the Pockels effect, makes it promising for optical modulators. These devices use electrical signals to control light and encode information onto it.

The difficulty is that a BTO crystal can contain small regions, called domains, with different crystal orientations. Those regions can interact with light differently, so measuring them together blends their responses. That makes it harder to determine the material’s underlying optical properties and predict how it will behave in a device.

To reduce that mixing, the team led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering examined two types of single-crystal BTO samples with relatively uniform domain orientations. The researchers used Mueller-matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry, a technique that measures changes in light’s polarization, or the orientation of its electric-field vibrations, when it reflects from or passes through a material. Those changes provide information about how the material affects light.

Their analysis covered wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), spanning the ultraviolet to the far-infrared. Because BTO interacts with light differently across that range, the researchers divided it into three spectral regions and used an analytical approach suited to each. They determined how the refractive index and absorption properties vary with both wavelength and crystal orientation.

The team also developed a method for calculating the overall optical response of a crystal containing differently oriented domains. Using the orientations and relative proportions of those domains, the method accounts for the mixed internal structure that had made BTO’s properties difficult to establish.

Even in the wavelength range where BTO is nearly transparent, the researchers were able to quantify very weak absorption. They combined ellipsometry with separate transmittance measurements, which record how much light passes through a sample, to determine extinction coefficients as low as approximately 10⁻⁵ in the 2–10 μm range. The extinction coefficient describes how strongly a material absorbs light, with smaller values indicating weaker absorption.

Together, these measurements help answer two practical questions about a waveguide, a structure that guides light through a device. The refractive index helps designers predict how the light will travel, while the extinction coefficient helps them estimate how much will be lost to absorption. Engineers can use the data to assess devices of different sizes and shapes before fabrication. Potential applications include communications modulators, devices that generate light at new wavelengths, and circuits that process quantum information using light.

KAIST, led by President Choongsik Bae, announced the work on November 8. The study was conducted in collaboration with Professor Harry A. Atwater’s team at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co.

“This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light,” said Professor Min Seok Jang. He added that the findings are expected to contribute to optical communication devices that reduce light loss and enable faster data transmission, as well as quantum photonic devices that require precise control of light.

Reference: “Broadband Optical Characterization of Tetragonal Barium Titanate by Mueller-Matrix Spectroscopic Ellipsometry” by Jiwon Kang, Nina Hong, Christopher M. Yi, Yun Su Go, Martin Thomaschewski, Hwi Je Woo, Prachi Thureja, Junghoon Jahng, Harry A. Atwater and Min Seok Jang, 20 October 2026, ACS Photonics. DOI: 10.1021/acsphotonics.6c01514

This research was supported by the Culture, Sports and Tourism R&D Program through the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), with funding from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism; the Basic Science Research Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), with funding from the Ministry of Education; the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR).

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

#6333. A Simple Pill Could Cure a Common Cause of High Blood Pressure

Blood pressure stayed lower for up to two years after treatment ended in a small follow-up study, suggesting some people with hormone-driven hypertension could avoid lifelong medication.

For people with a common hormonal cause of high blood pressure, a cure has required surgery to remove an entire adrenal gland. Medication can keep their blood pressure under control, often with the prospect of taking it for life.

The condition, called primary aldosteronism, accounts for an estimated 5% to 10% of cases of high blood pressure, or hypertension, which affects millions of people worldwide. Benign nodules in the adrenal glands produce too much of the hormone aldosterone, causing the kidneys to retain excess salt and driving blood pressure up.

A study led by Queen Mary University of London now suggests that a limited course of medication could offer a lasting cure for some people with this condition. The approach, called extended aldosterone synthase inhibition (EASI), involves taking a new class of drugs for 6 to 12 months. These drugs block aldosterone synthase, an enzyme needed to make the hormone, targeting the excess production responsible for the hypertension.

The findings, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, came from follow-up measurements in 14 people treated at eight centers across the United States. They had participated in the first study of this drug class in people with primary aldosteronism, also led by Queen Mary and reported last year in the same journal. Researchers subsequently examined routine measurements of their blood pressure and hormone levels to see how they compared with values recorded before treatment.

For up to two years after treatment ended, hormone levels and blood pressure remained similar to, or lower than, those measured while participants were taking the drugs. The main marker of excess aldosterone production remained 99% below its pretreatment level, and blood pressure was, on average, 25 points lower. Researchers reported partial or complete resolution of hypertension, with almost a quarter of participants having normal blood pressure without taking any other medication.

Mason Freeman, Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, initiated the original study while medical director at Cincor. He said, “This follow-up study led by Dr. Brown has generated some extraordinary and unexpected findings. The sustained remission in the biochemical markers of the hyperaldosterone state, combined with much improved blood pressure levels, offers the very exciting possibility that many patients with primary aldosteronism may be able to be treated with a once-a-day pill, perhaps for a limited period of time, and obtain similar benefits to what we now achieve only after invasive diagnostic testing and major adrenal surgery.”

Aldosterone synthase inhibitors had previously been tested in larger studies of people with hypertension. Those studies generally involved shorter treatment periods of 6 to 12 weeks, with outcomes measured while people were still taking the medication. Following patients after a 6- to 12-month course revealed the possibility that the treatment’s effects could outlast the medication itself.

One possible explanation dates to a 2005 experiment in mice. When scientists deleted the gene responsible for producing aldosterone synthase, the cells that make aldosterone disappeared. Researchers at Queen Mary predicted that blocking the enzyme for a prolonged period might have a similar effect in humans, potentially removing the source of excess hormone production.

Morris Brown, the study’s lead author and Professor of Endocrine Hypertension at Queen Mary, said, “While duly cautious about our findings because of the pragmatic nature of the study, they were predicted by previous experiments, and longer follow-up may justify a claim that a finite course of medication leads to infinite cure.

“EASI-treatment is unlikely to be the elixir for most patients with hypertension. But the possibility of tablets achieving a surgical cure has long been a holy grail for this common type of hypertension.”

The researchers are now leading a larger prospective clinical trial called ELIXIR to investigate whether EASI treatment can provide a lasting cure for people with primary aldosteronism. The trial will also use molecular imaging of the adrenal glands to examine whether prolonged treatment causes aldosterone-producing cells to disappear in humans.

Reference: “Hyperaldosteronism Remission after Extended Aldosterone Synthase Inhibition” by Morris J. Brown, Adina F. Turcu, Ramin Sam, Lawrence S. Kirschner, Oksana Hamidi, Aysegul Eren, Anat Ben-Shlomo, Wenyu Huang, Irina Bancos, Amir H. Hamrahian and Mason W. Freeman, 6 November 2026, New England Journal of Medicine. DOI: 10.1056/NEJMc2611265

#6332. The 5 Best Gas Snowblowers Can Move Mountains (of Snow)

Too much snow to shovel? A snowblower offers the most power and the longest runtime.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter will be here before you know it, which means the best time to prepare for cold weather and potential snowstorms is now. While snowfall isn't as regular in many parts of the country as it used to be, storm systems can still dump big piles of snow at once. When it comes time to dig out, there are few tools as effective as a gas-powered snowblower.

Although electric snowblowers are certainly attractive—they are relatively lightweight, easy to use, and require little maintenance—they lack the raw power and long runtime you’ll need if a storm drops 18 inches of snow or more on your home, especially if you have a large driveway.

The best gas snowblowers can carve a path as wide as two feet—giving you plenty of room to walk through as much as 21 inches of snow on a single pass. And if you keep a spare tank handy, you should have more than enough runtime to clear your walks and driveway multiple times. If you’re in the market for a heavy-duty snow removal machine, we’ve researched and tested plenty. These are our top picks, plus a breakdown of everything you need to know to pick out the best gas snowblower for your home.

If you have a large driveway and get a lot of snow, this is the machine you want. This big Ariens has a 30-inch-wide clearing path and an ideal clearing depth of 18 inches. Its four-stroke gas engine means no fussing with mixed fuel, and the push-button electric start means you don't have to exhaust yourself with a recoil starter.

This is a stout machine that is made for working. Test Editor Brad Ford runs a similar machine on his property, which is extra demanding because he has a gravel driveway. Thankfully, this machine can handle gravel surfaces thanks to its adjustable skid shoes, which allow extra clearance between the base of the auger and the driveway.

This machine is not for everybody; smaller properties will be well-served by the smaller picks below. But for those with the capacity for this kind of snowblower, this Ariens is a solid choice.

This model from Champion Power Equipment lists at $899, which is a good price point considering many two-stage snowblowers are more than $1,000. But it’s not short on features. This model gives you push-button electric start, a self-propelled drive system, remote chute control, and an LED headlight for clearing snow at night. After all, the snow doesn’t always stop falling during work hours.

It also handles fairly deep snowfall with a 24-inch width and a 20.5-inch height. To help keep the blades safe on uneven terrain, you can adjust the height to handle that, or clear areas like gravel paths. Another feature we really like is the ability to turn the wheels 180 degrees to help make tighter turns. Features like that can’t always be found at this price point, which is why it’s our pick for a snowblower that packs a lot of value.

A medium-sized property that only gets a moderate amount of guaranteed snowfall each year doesn’t need a two-stage snowblower. A single-stage model is fully capable of clearing your driveway and sidewalks. This model from Toro has plenty of power to get that job done, with a 212-cc engine that should cut through even wet snow and throw it up to 35 feet away. This model is also self-propelled to help you do the pushing.

Some of the features we like on it are a trigger and slide that can change the direction of the discharge chute from the handle and a push-button electric start—both make operating it a little bit easier.

Like most single-stage snowblowers, its intake is lower than a two-stage, so you can only expect to clear snowfall up to 10 inches. If you commonly get much higher than that, you’ll want a more robust snowblower, but if you only have a few moderate snow events each winter, this Toro will get the job done.

The Toro SnowMaster 824 QXE stands apart from other single-stage gas snowblowers because of its intuitive controls and powerful engine. With a 252-cc engine, it chews rapidly through snow, carving a 24-inch path through banks up to 18 inches high.

With a lighter, more compact frame and automatic steering, the 824 QXE is easier to maneuver than its dual-stage counterparts. And, unlike most single-stage snowblowers, the auger is slightly elevated, so you can use it on gravel surfaces without having to worry about sucking rocks into it.

This machine also brings lots of special features to make the clearing process easier. Not only is it self-propelled, but it features a “personal pace system” that automatically adjusts the snowblower’s speed to match your walking pace, so you don’t have to fumble with speed controls. If you're familiar with Toro's self-propelled lawn mowers, this system should be familiar.

The snowblower also has a push-button starter and joystick-operated chute control, which makes it easy to adjust your snow output on the fly. If you’re looking for a snowblower to clear up to 18 inches of snow from a small to medium-sized driveway, the SnowMaster 824 QXE is a worthy choice.

This snowblower from Murray is another great example of a two-stage snowblower from a respected company that doesn’t cost more than $1,000. It doesn’t have some of the extra features like our best value pick—namely, a headlight and a 180-degree wheel rotation—but it otherwise matches it in size and power.

It also has all the primary features you would want, including an adjustable chute that lets you aim the snow where you want, push-button electric start, an auger that can propel snow up to 40 feet away, and a self-propel drive with six forward speeds and two reverse speeds.

Something unique to the model, however, is a set of 15-inch snow-terrain tires that handle icy and rocky conditions better than others. Wheels are something other brands can skimp on, but Murray hasn’t done that here. If you have gravel paths or older sidewalks that present a challenge, this model is likely up to the task.

Gas snowblowers are the best tools for heavy-duty snow removal jobs at home. They’re effective against snowbanks piled up to two feet high, and can clear out larger areas, including wide driveways and walking paths. If you live somewhere that gets hit by many large snowstorms each season, and you’ve got a considerable-sized area to clear, then this is what you need.

Not everyone needs a gas snowblower, though. For homes with smaller needs, they may feel like more trouble than they’re worth. Gas-powered machines require more maintenance. Plus, they’re usually quite heavy, which makes them hard to use on tiered walkways with steps. If heavy snow is a rare occurrence, we’d recommend going with an electric snowblower instead, which will be more nimble and won’t produce any fumes.

Most gas snowblowers feature either a single-stage or two-stage mechanism, depending on how the snowblower collects, processes, and expels snow.

Also known as “snow throwers,” they use an auger to pull in snow, break it up, and throw the snow out through the chute in a single action.

These also use an auger to pull in snow, but then mash it up with a spinning impeller before spitting it out through the chute. Separating the snow-pulling and snow-crushing/throwing mechanisms allows the two-stage snowblowers to move snow more quickly and throw it a longer distance, which can be helpful when clearing larger driveways. These robust machines also work better on gravel, since their augers are slightly elevated and won’t draw rocks into the tines.

With an extra component that requires a more powerful engine to operate properly, two-stage snowblowers are generally larger, making them more difficult to maneuver around tight spaces. If you have a small walkway or gardens with uneven ground to avoid, operating one may feel unwieldy. As you might expect, they also cost more than their single-stage counterparts.

As with deciding between electric and gas snowblowers, consider the size of the area you normally clear before picking a single- or two-stage model. Single-stage snowblowers work well for clearing walking paths and the average-sized two- to four-car paved driveway. Dual-stage models are ideal for clearing deep snow from long paved or gravel driveways.

A snowblower’s clearing width and intake height determine how much snow it can move with each pass. The larger the snowblower’s intake, the more quickly you can get the job done.

Most single-stage gas-powered snowblowers have intakes that range from 22 to 24 inches wide, while two-stage snowblowers can have intakes that are up to 32 inches wide. The height of the snowblower’s intake, which is sometimes referred to as “clearing depth,” indicates the maximum snow depth it can handle. The intake height for a gas snowblower ranges from 18 to 21 inches.

Purchasing the snowblower with the widest, tallest intake may seem like a no-brainer, but keep in mind that there’s a correlation between intake dimensions and the overall size of the snowblower. The largest gas snowblowers will have a harder time maneuvering through tight turns. Ultimately, you should choose the smallest option that can effectively clear the paths you need and the amount of snow you expect to see.

A snowblower's job is to take snow in front of you and move it somewhere out of the way. With a more powerful snowblower, you can send the snow farther away. That’s crucial when you’re clearing out a large space, and you need to pile it up dozens of feet from you. Single-stage gas snowblowers can launch snow up to 40 feet, while two-stage snowblowers have a snow-throwing range of 50 feet or more.

Some gas snowblowers come equipped with a throttle on the dashboard that allows you to adjust the throwing distance by changing the speed of the impeller, allowing you to target a specific snow-piling plot.

Beyond the basics, many gas snowblowers have additional features that make them easier to use. Since they weigh hundreds of pounds, many are self-propelled, so you don’t have to push them forward. Most also have electric starters that eliminate the need to pull a starter cord. Some even have built-in power steering that automatically slows one wheel for easy turning.

Other quality-of-life features abound: You may find dashboard controls that allow you to change the chute direction and snowblower speed with one hand, LED headlights for late-night (or early morning) jobs, and handlebars that heat up to keep your hands nice and toasty as you work.

We selected the best gas snowblowers based on recommendations from the Popular Mechanics test team, as well as research and personal testing experience. Some of our picks were recommended by Popular Mechanics test editor Brad Ford, who has logged hours and hours testing snowblowers over the years. The final lineup includes a mix of single-stage gas-powered models for small to moderate driveways that can house four to six cars, and larger two-stage models that can clear snow from the longer and larger driveways you usually find on rural properties.

There are a few things you need to do to make sure your gas snowblower runs smoothly through the season:

First, check the oil level between each use and top off as needed. You should change the oil once a year, even if you didn’t use your snowblower all winter.

Change the spark plug at the beginning of each season to ensure it starts smoothly. A dirty spark plug can make it difficult to get your snowblower going, especially in extreme cold.

Lastly, small gas engines require plenty of airflow to run smoothly, so check the air filter once a season and replace it if it's dirty.

Snowblowers use unleaded gasoline—the same thing you put in your car—which begins to degrade after about 60 days. Running a snowblower with old fuel can clog the carburetor and make the engine hard to start, so you should never store your snowblower with fuel left in the tank.

Before putting your snowblower to bed for the season, either run the fuel tank dry or add fuel stabilizer, which keeps gasoline fresh for up to 24 months, to the tank. If you use fuel stabilizer, run the snowblower for a minute or two after adding it to the tank to circulate it through the engine.

A snowblower should be able to handle the lion’s share of your snow removal duties, but you should definitely keep a snow shovel around to clean up whatever the snowblower leaves behind. You may also want to save the gas and dig out with a shovel after a light, soft snowfall.

#6331. Scientists Develop Injectable Glucose Sensor That Could Change Diabetes Care

An experimental injectable sensor could give people with diabetes a more affordable way to track blood sugar, with early tests showing that a cheaper sensing ingredient performed similarly to its costlier alternative.

For millions of people with diabetes, knowing how glucose levels are changing helps guide decisions about medication, meals, and daily activities. Continuous glucose monitors provide that information in real time, but their cost keeps the devices out of reach for some patients. Making monitoring more affordable requires attention to the materials inside a sensor, as well as how reliably they work.

Researchers at Texas A&M University have identified a less expensive ingredient for an experimental injectable glucose sensor. Their study, published in ACS Measurement Science AU, found that a sensing material costing roughly one-tenth as much as an alternative used in earlier versions delivered comparable performance.

The proposed sensor houses its sensing chemistry in a small hydrogel, a water-rich material that can be injected into tissue and sit beneath the skin. The gel provides a stable home for the sensing materials while allowing glucose to pass through. In testing, it retained more than 94% of the sensing mixture over seven days, demonstrating that the chemistry could function within an injectable platform.

“Our long-term goal is to develop a reliable, affordable injectable glucose sensor that can expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly for people in under-resourced communities and those without adequate insurance coverage,” said Dr. Gérard L. Coté, the study’s principal investigator and a professor of biomedical engineering in Texas A&M’s College of Engineering. “Reducing the cost of the sensing materials is one step toward making these technologies accessible to more people who need them.”

To measure glucose, the platform uses changes in near-infrared fluorescence, a light signal beyond the visible range. Many glucose-monitoring systems rely on enzymes, which help chemical reactions occur. This approach instead detects glucose through a competition between molecules.

Glucose and a fluorescent sugar compound compete for available binding sites on a protein called concanavalin A, or ConA. As glucose concentrations rise, more glucose molecules enter that competition, changing the fluorescent signal. This process, known as competitive binding, allows the researchers to track glucose concentrations without enzymes.

The team compared several glucose-binding compounds, including two forms of a sugar called mannopentaose. Earlier versions of the technology used α-mannopentaose. The much less expensive β-mannopentaose provided comparable sensing performance and also performed well in artificial interstitial fluid, a solution designed to mimic the environment beneath the skin.

“The surprising part was how closely the lower-cost material matched the performance of the more expensive alternative,” said Dr. Sayantan Tripathy, an assistant research scientist in Texas A&M’s Optical and Bio-Sensing Laboratory and the study’s lead author. “In this case, the cheaper option wasn’t really a compromise, and that’s an important finding when you’re thinking about future glucose-monitoring technologies.”

The cost comparison concerns one sensing component. The technology remains at the proof-of-concept stage and needs additional development and testing before it could be considered for clinical use.

“Developing an affordable glucose sensor means considering the cost of the individual materials as well as how well they work together,” Coté said. “This study shows that we can substantially reduce the cost of one sensing component while maintaining comparable performance, giving us a promising foundation for further development.”

Reducing manufacturing costs could eventually help expand access to future diabetes-monitoring technologies. That possibility makes affordability a consideration throughout development, alongside technical performance.

“When new medical technologies are expensive, access can be limited,” said Dr. Melissa Grunlan, a study co-author, professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering, and professor of chemistry in the College of Arts and Sciences. “Our goal is to develop sensors that are not only effective but affordable for the people who rely on them.”

The team plans to refine the platform and evaluate additional components that may improve its performance, longevity, and practicality.

“While the work remains in the research stage, the findings suggest that future glucose-monitoring technologies may not have to rely on expensive materials to deliver effective results,” Tripathy said.

Reference: “β-Anomeric Mannopentaose-Based Nonenzymatic NIR Glucose Sensor Enabling Cost-Effective Continuous Monitoring” by Sayantan Tripathy, Diana Al Husseini, Carolina I. Martinez, Anthony Dongchau, Samyucktha Ganesapandian, Melissa A Grunlan and Gerard L Cote, 19 August 2026, ACS Measurement Science Au. DOI: 10.1021/acsmeasuresciau.6c00076
