#6303. Researchers Turn Moon Dust Into LEGO-Like Bricks That Could Build Future Lunar Bases

Building on the Moon could require fewer supplies from Earth, as scientists have found a way to fuse simulated lunar dust into interlocking bricks without added materials.

Building a future home on the Moon might someday resemble assembling a giant LEGO set. Instead of plastic pieces, astronauts could use interlocking bricks made from lunar dust, creating structures from materials already available on the Moon’s surface.

Researchers at the University of Arkansas have taken an early step toward that possibility by demonstrating that simulated lunar dust can be 3D-printed into LEGO-like building blocks without adding other materials. The approach could reduce the construction supplies NASA would need to transport from Earth as it works toward establishing permanent settlements on the Moon.

The key ingredient is lunar regolith, the loose, dusty material covering the Moon’s surface. Unlike soil on Earth, regolith contains no organic matter. It consists of jagged particles formed over billions of years as asteroids, micrometeorites, and other space debris struck the Moon.

For their experiments, the researchers used Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercially available material designed to imitate samples collected during the Apollo missions in the 1960s and early 1970s.

The study, published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, then an undergraduate at the University of Arkansas, and senior author Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering.

To create the bricks, the team used a 3D-printing technique called laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source, such as a laser, heats selected portions of the powder, causing the particles to bond together through a process known as sintering. The printing bed then lowers, allowing another layer of powder to be added. Repeating these steps gradually builds a three-dimensional object.

Other researchers have successfully printed objects using lunar regolith mixed with binding agents. However, those additional ingredients would have to be transported from Earth, increasing the amount of material needed for construction on the Moon.

The Arkansas team demonstrated for the first time that simulated lunar regolith could be sintered directly into reconfigurable construction blocks without a binder, using a relatively low-power light source.

“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said.

The researchers produced blocks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. These shapes could fit together much like LEGO bricks, allowing individual pieces to be assembled into larger structures.

Although the researchers successfully created interlocking blocks, the material is not yet strong enough for all the demands of lunar construction. Bricks made entirely from simulated regolith were more porous and structurally weaker than objects printed with binding agents.

“These structures we’re making can be self-supported,” McCallum said. “But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet.”

The team must also determine how the printing process would behave under actual lunar conditions. According to Shou, further experiments are needed to understand its performance in microgravity and vacuum environments, while improvements to the bricks’ mechanical properties will be necessary before they become practical construction materials.

Shou remains optimistic that the approach could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture components and structures for permanent settlements on the Moon.

For McCallum, the project also marked an important early step in his scientific career. A native of Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou’s laboratory early in his undergraduate studies, encouraged by his professor’s commitment to involving students in research.

“He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research,” McCallum said.

McCallum graduated in May with degrees in mechanical engineering and physics. He was subsequently awarded an inaugural Lafayette Fellowship, a program established to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the United States. Only 30 fellows were selected from more than 3,400 applicants to pursue master’s degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-SUPAERO), one of France’s leading aerospace engineering schools.

Although his academic focus has shifted away from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou’s laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with teaching him how to navigate the challenges of scientific investigation.

“It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through,” he said. “It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.”

Reference: “Additive manufacturing of lunar regolith for reconfigurable building blocks toward lunar habitation” by Cole McCallum, Youwen Liang, Nahid Tushar, Ben Xu, Bo Zhao, Hao Zeng and Wan Shou, 29 August 2026, npj Advanced Manufacturing. DOI: 10.1038/s44334-026-00111-x

This work was supported by the Honors College Undergraduate Research Grant to C.M. and the Startup Package from the University of Arkansas to W.S.

#6302. Tadpoles are dying in waves in Brazil, and scientists have found a clue

Scientists linked recurring tadpole deaths in a Brazilian pond to ranavirus, with outbreaks more likely after weeks of low humidity.

Before January 2024, the only tadpole deaths recorded at a small pond in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest were isolated cases involving predators.

Since then deaths at the pond have occurred in repeated waves. Outbreaks were reported in three consecutive breeding seasons.

According to the research team, the cause was ranavirus. This virus is known to infect amphibians and reptiles as well as fish. Outbreaks were found to be more likely after periods in which the air had been dry for some weeks.

Most of the dead tadpoles (315 of 324) belonged to the monkey frog (Phyllomedusa distincta). This leaf frog is found only in the Atlantic Forest.

The authors reported that this was the first confirmed ranavirus die-off among wild native amphibians in the American tropics.

Researchers also recorded a sharp decline in egg-laying compared with counts from two decades earlier.

The authors believe the virus is the most likely explanation for the decline. A gap of more than 20 years in the egg counts makes a direct link difficult to establish.

The study was carried out by Aline Fonseca as part of her doctoral research at the Federal University of Paraná (UFPR).

Her colleagues included the owners of the reserve: Germano Woehl Jr. and Elza Nishimura Woehl of the Rã-Bugio Institute.

The work took place at the Rã-Bugio Sanctuary, a protected reserve of about 12 acres (4.75 hectares) in Guaramirim in the state of Santa Catarina.

The pond itself is fed by two springs. It is roughly two-thirds the size of a tennis court and has been kept free of fish so that frogs are able to breed in it.

Monkey frog tadpoles tend to hang upright at the surface of the water. As a result, dead tadpoles were relatively easy to find and count.

Three outbreak periods were recorded. The first ran from January to April 2024 and the second from November 2024 to January 2025. The third lasted from late November 2025 to March 2026.

Of the 324 dead tadpoles that were collected, 315 were monkey frogs and nine were Bischoff’s tree frogs (Boana bischoffi). Ranavirus DNA was detected in 287 of them (about 89%).

Redness and swelling were commonly observed in the infected tadpoles along with bleeding beneath the skin. Bleeding inside the eye was noted in some individuals.

The presence of a virus in a dead animal does not by itself establish the cause of death.

Liver tissue from 13 infected tadpoles was therefore also examined under a microscope and large areas of dead cells were found.

No sick tadpoles were observed in a second pond that lies about 1,500 feet (450 meters) away and is separated from the first by intact forest.

Measurements made at the affected pond during the first outbreak showed that water acidity was normal. No signs of contamination were detected.

On several occasions the discovery of a first dead tadpole was followed within a short time by many more.

Tadpoles that were dying were seen floating at the surface and were unable to swim down. In most cases, death followed within 30 minutes.

Tadpoles that hatched early or late in the breeding season survived better than those that hatched in the middle of it.

The pond was most crowded in the middle of the breeding season, when nearly all tadpoles died.

Most of the bodies that were recovered belonged to young tadpoles whose back legs had only begun to form.

However, older tadpoles carried about the same amount of virus. This suggests that heavier infection was not the reason the young made up most of the dead.

The authors believe timing is a more likely explanation. Most tadpoles in the pond were still young when the outbreaks occurred.

It is also possible that larger dead tadpoles were eaten by predators and scavengers before they could be counted.

Monkey frogs lay their eggs on leaves above the water.

The female folds each leaf around the clutch (a group of eggs). When the eggs hatch, the tadpoles drop into the pond below.

Between August 1999 and February 2004, the Woehls searched leaves, stems and tree trunks around the pond every morning during the breeding season.

Each new clutch was marked so that it would not be counted twice.

The same daily counts were repeated from August 2025 to February 2026 after the second outbreak season.

Egg-laying was estimated to have fallen by about 83% (with the likely decline lying between 70% and 90%).

Clutch counts were lower throughout the breeding season.

The decline therefore could not be explained by a change in the timing of laying.

The researchers suggest that fewer young frogs surviving to adulthood could help explain the decline in egg-laying.

Daily records from the three outbreak seasons were compared with weather data. Humidity (the amount of moisture in the air) was found to be the strongest predictor of deaths.

Temperature did not help to predict them. Rainfall added no further information once humidity had been taken into account.

When average humidity over the previous two weeks was 65%, the team’s model estimated a nearly 98% chance of finding dead tadpoles on a given day. When it was 90%, the estimate fell to about 7%.

“The virus is likely present in the environment at all times without causing disease, but low humidity may cause it to increase its own replication and trigger an outbreak,” Fonseca said.

As water levels fall the tadpoles are crowded into less space. This may make it easier for the virus to spread between them.

It has also been suggested by the authors that dry conditions may place the animals under stress and weaken their immune defenses.

Dry weeks may help to explain when outbreaks occurred.

But the researchers also had to consider whether longer-term changes in the weather could account for the decline in egg-laying.

For this reason, weather records covering the period from 1999 to 2026 were examined.

No clear long-term trend was detected in temperature or rainfall or humidity. Average temperature rose by about 0.27°F (0.15°C) per decade.

This increase was not statistically significant. The records therefore did not establish a clear warming trend.

Whether egg counts came from before or after the outbreaks explained the decline better than any of the weather measures. Adding weather data to that comparison improved it only slightly.

It should be noted that the weather data were not collected at the pond. They were taken from a global dataset in which each area measures about 7 by 6 miles (11 by 10 km).

No clutch counts were made between 2004 and 2025. As a result the point at which the decline began cannot be determined.

Although no signs of pollution were found at the reserve, other threats to the frogs cannot be ruled out.

Ranavirus is regarded by the authors as the strongest explanation for the fall in egg-laying. But it has not been shown to be the cause.

Six stretches of the virus’s genes were sequenced and were found to be identical in every sample analyzed. All of them matched the frog virus 3 group.

That group is known to infect amphibians and reptiles and fish on several continents. Because the match is so close, the origin of the outbreak is difficult to trace.

Ranavirus has previously killed wood frog tadpoles in North America. In South America most confirmed die-offs had until now involved bullfrogs raised on farms.

Frog virus 3 has caused repeated losses at farms in the Atlantic Forest region that raise American bullfrogs.

The authors suggest that wastewater from crowded farms could carry the virus into wild ponds. It has not been established that this occurred at the reserve.

The virus may have arrived in the forest recently, or it may have been present for many years.

Co-author Luís Felipe Toledo of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) has spent more than a decade studying chytrid fungus.

The fungus is another threat to amphibians. His group has found evidence of the fungus on Brazilian amphibians dating back to 1916.

“Perhaps the ranavirus has also been here for a long time. It remains to be seen what changed for it to become a threat,” Toledo said.

Climate forecasts for the Atlantic Forest indicate that droughts are likely to become more frequent and more severe.

The authors warn that if dry weeks do help to trigger these outbreaks then losses of this kind could occur more often and become more serious.

The UFPR team plans to collect samples from nearby areas in order to find out where else the virus is present. Toledo has also pointed to museum collections as a possible source of clues.

Testing preserved frogs could help to establish how long ranavirus has been in the region.

The study is published in the journal Biodiversity and Conservation.

#6301. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

W. Xiong et al. Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space. Science. 2026. doi: 10.1126/science.aea5324N. Gaaloul et al. A space-based quantum gas laboratory at picokelvin energy scales. Nature Communications. 2022. doi: 10.1038/s41467-022-35274-6C. Deppner et al. Collective-mode enhanced matter-wave optics. Physical Review Letters. 2021. doi: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.100401

#6299. “A Magnetar Is Born”: Supercomputer Simulates One of the Universe’s Most Violent Collisions

A black hole isn’t the only possible outcome when neutron stars collide: simulations suggest some mergers can create the extreme magnetic fields of magnetars in milliseconds.

When two neutron stars collide, the result is often a black hole. But some mergers leave behind a massive neutron star with an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field. New supercomputer simulations suggest that these collisions can produce magnetar-strength magnetic fields in just milliseconds, offering a possible explanation for how some of the universe’s most magnetic objects form.

Magnetars are a rare class of neutron stars, distinguished by magnetic fields that can be roughly 1,000 times stronger than those of ordinary neutron stars. They are associated with intense bursts of radiation, including soft gamma-ray repeaters, and may also produce some fast radio bursts.

Using Japan’s FUGAKU supercomputer, researchers simulated the collision of two neutron stars, each with 1.35 times the Sun’s mass. The calculation achieved a spatial resolution of 6.25 meters (20.5 feet), allowing the team to track small-scale turbulence and its effects on magnetic fields throughout the merger.

The stars initially had magnetic fields of approximately 3.16 trillion gauss, consistent with the upper range observed in binary pulsars. The collision generated fields reaching around 10 quadrillion gauss across parts of the remnant, with localized regions reaching even greater strengths.

The researchers say the simulation demonstrates that “the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability that emerges when the two neutron stars touch amplifies the magnetic field to an expected electromagnetic saturation energy of ∼ 10⁵⁰ erg within 3 ms after the merger.”

The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability develops when neighboring layers of fluid move at different velocities. During a neutron star merger, enormous differences in fluid motion generate turbulence that stretches and strengthens magnetic fields.

Initially, the strongest amplification occurs on very small scales. The turbulent magnetic field subsequently influences progressively larger regions of the merged star, allowing magnetic amplification to reach stellar scales.

The researchers say the instability “induces stellar-scale magnetic field amplification by at least a factor of 316.”

Within approximately five milliseconds, the simulated stellar-scale magnetic field had increased from 3.16 trillion gauss to around one quadrillion gauss, reaching magnetar strength. As the researchers put it, “Namely, a magnetar is born.”

Although the simulation produced magnetar-strength fields, the researchers caution that uncertainties in how turbulence and magnetic dissipation operate at extremely small scales could affect the estimated amplification.

In one extrapolation to more realistic conditions, the simulated stellar-scale field could be overestimated by a factor of 10. Even under that assumption, the resulting magnetic field would still reach approximately 100 trillion gauss.

The magnetic structure also remained concentrated near the remnant’s equatorial plane rather than forming the organized polar field associated with launching relativistic jets. Additional magnetic processes, particularly the magnetorotational instability, may be needed to develop that configuration.

The researchers say their “result suggests that a magnetar formation could be inevitable in binary neutron star mergers at least temporarily following the mergers, unless it promptly collapses to a black hole.”

The simulations cover only the earliest moments after the collision. Longer calculations will be needed to determine how these magnetic fields evolve, whether they help power energetic outbursts, and how long the resulting neutron star can survive before potentially collapsing into a black hole.

Reference: “A magnetar formation in binary neutron star merger” by Kenta Kiuchi, Alexis Reboul-Salze, Yuichiro Sekiguchi and Masaru Shibata, June 9, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2606.11299

#6298. Webb captures a galaxy still reeling from an ancient collision

Webb’s infrared view of the Cartwheel Galaxy reveals how an ancient collision reshaped its structure and sparked waves of star formation.

Today’s Image of the Day features the Cartwheel Galaxy, where a bright ring of stars surrounds a glowing center and curved strands of dust stretch between them like spokes.

The striking shape emerged from a violent collision that disrupted a spiral galaxy hundreds of millions of years ago.

New stars now shine along the outer ring, while traces of the galaxy’s earlier structure remain woven through the scene.

The view comes from the James Webb Space Telescope, which combined observations from two infrared instruments to reveal stars and dust in extraordinary detail.

Released on August 2, 2022, the image also includes two smaller companion galaxies and a background scattered with more distant galaxies.

Located roughly 500 million light-years away in the constellation Sculptor, the Cartwheel belongs to an unusual class known as ring galaxies.

Its appearance differs sharply from the familiar spiral arms of our Milky Way.

Astronomers attribute that shape to a high-speed collision between a large spiral galaxy and a smaller galaxy.

The smaller galaxy responsible for the impact is outside this image, so neither of the two prominent companions should be mistaken for the intruder.

The encounter sent disturbances outward through the larger galaxy, producing a bright inner ring and a much broader outer ring.

NASA compares their expansion to ripples spreading across a pond after a stone hits the water.

Those enormous ripples have reshaped the galaxy over hundreds of millions of years. What appears to be a finished wheel is still undergoing change.

The outer ring marks a region where the collision’s effects continue to unfold. As it expands into surrounding gas, it triggers the formation of new stars.

NASA estimates that this outer structure has been expanding for about 440 million years.

Star formation and supernovas, the explosions of dying stars, help make it an especially active part of the galaxy.

The center has its own concentrations of activity. Hot dust fills the bright core, and its most luminous areas contain enormous clusters of young stars.

Together, these regions show how a galactic collision can do more than rearrange existing material.

It can also change where new generations of stars emerge, leaving a pattern that remains visible long after the original encounter.

Earlier observations, including images from the Hubble Space Telescope, had already revealed the Cartwheel’s unusual structure. But dust obscures parts of the galaxy when viewed in visible light.

Webb observes infrared wavelengths, allowing astronomers to examine stars that are harder to distinguish through that dusty veil.

Its Near-Infrared Camera, or NIRCam, reveals points of starlight and pockets of star formation.

It also helps distinguish the smoother distribution of older stars from the clumpier regions associated with younger populations.

The Mid-Infrared Instrument, known as MIRI, adds a different perspective by detecting emission from dust and revealing material rich in hydrocarbons and silicate compounds.

Combining the instruments brings the stellar populations and dusty structures into the same view.

Each contributes information that would be harder to recognize from the other instrument alone.

The image’s colors translate infrared observations into a form human eyes can see. They help separate different features rather than reproduce the view an astronaut would see through a window.

Blue points mark individual stars or regions of star formation.

Bright red strands trace glowing dust, including the curved spokes that connect the inner and outer portions of the galaxy.

Those spokes preserve something of the spiral galaxy that existed before the collision.

Despite the disruption, the Cartwheel retained rotating arms, linking its present appearance to its earlier form.

Similar glowing dust also appears in the companion spiral galaxy toward the upper left, giving viewers another structure to explore beyond the dominant ring.

The Cartwheel’s eventual shape remains uncertain.

Its expanding rings and surviving spiral features capture a galaxy in transition, with its past still visible inside the changes set in motion by the collision.

That makes the image more than a portrait of an unusual object.

Across its bright rim and dusty spokes, the Cartwheel records how one encounter can influence a galaxy for hundreds of millions of years.

The collision has passed. The galaxy is still responding.

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

#6296. After Testing Bose and Denon, I’m Convinced the Sonos Beam Ultra Is the Best Small Soundbar

Between its Beam and Arc Ultra soundbars, Sonos finds a new, more compact sweet spot.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar is the whole-home audio brand’s attempt to find a middle ground in the home theater space. Wedged between its compact Sonos Beam and flagship Arc Ultra soundbar, the Beam Ultra sits in the middle in terms of size, power, and price.

That’s an intriguing proposition: The Beam Ultra has many of the advanced features I loved in the Arc Ultra, including Dolby Atmos with up-firing speakers and A.I.-powered speech enhancement to boost dialogue in the mix. But the Arc Ultra is made for big TVs and carries a $1,099 price tag: It’s an upgrade for serious home theater fans with a big budget. At $699, the Beam Ultra is still a serious investment, but seems far more attainable than the tubular Arc.

And, after a few weeks of testing, I feel comfortable saying that Beam Ultra sounds more like the Arc Ultra’s little brother than a slightly bigger Beam. Its stellar audio performance, which I’ll break down shortly, deserves the Ultra name. And the Beam Ultra delivers it in a much smaller footprint than the Arc Ultra—at about 30 inches wide, it’s only 4 inches wider than the second-generation Beam, but more than a foot narrower than the Arc Ultra.

If you are a serious cinephile with the budget to upgrade, but don’t have a stand or space to accommodate a full-size soundbar, the Sonos Beam Ultra almost certainly sets a new gold standard for compact soundbars, delivering top-tier audio with minimal compromises.

Compared to other small soundbars, the Sonos Beam Ultra has tremendous firepower behind it, which may explain why it sounds bigger than it is. It’s a 7.1.2 system, which means it has seven forward-facing speakers, a single down-firing unit, and two up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos virtual surround sound. That’s more than the Bose Smart Soundbar (five audio drivers in a 3.0.2-channel layout) and the Denon Home 550, which I previously would’ve called the top compact options in the space.

More audio drivers don't automatically mean better sound. Still, they do let the Beam Ultra project a wider soundstage and reduce the number of audio channels that need to be combined and condensed. The results are, in a word, powerful. It generates an impressive soundstage, simultaneously expansive and precise. It is certainly more immersive and capable than any soundbar I’ve ever considered describing as “compact.”

At the same time, it can convey incredible nuance. The eclectic selection of music I played—from bass-heavy downtempo tracks to classical jazz albums—came through with clear separation across bass, treble, and midrange, unlike lesser-equipped alternatives from other makers. For folks who plan to stream music from their phone, the Beam Ultra supports lossless audio files and can play them over WiFi without compression. (If you connect your soundbar to your phone via Bluetooth, you'll get some audio degradation, whether the soundbar supports lossless or not.)

The more varied your audio diet, the more important it is to fine-tune the soundbar with EQ settings that match the music, movies, sports, or video games you’re listening to. The Sonos companion app makes it easy to swap modes or tweak settings on-the-fly, including the height of the sound from the up-firing speakers. This trick can further enhance scenes in Dolby Atmos content, especially action sequences (e.g., explosions, flying aircraft, etc.).

You can also adjust advanced features like Sonos’s signature AI-powered voice enhancement. The voice-enhancement feature, which was introduced in the Arc Ultra, works wonders when you’re watching movies or sports, cranking up the volume and clarity of dialogue amid other sounds so you can hear clearly. The feature comes with some drawbacks: Cranking up voice enhancement to “high” takes a toll on overall sound quality. I would avoid going above “medium.” This was not specific to Beam Ultra, though; I experienced similar issues with the Arc Ultra as well.

Beyond audio playback via the Sonos platform, the Beam Ultra soundbar supports Apple AirPlay 2 for streaming audio from an iPhone, a MacBook, or an iPad. Basic Bluetooth is built in, just in case, and, to my surprise, you can also connect a device directly to the soundbar via a USB-C cable.

Like the Arc Ultra soundbar, the Beam Ultra can deliver a truly private Dolby Atmos audio experience by connecting to the excellent Sonos Ace and Ace Ultra wireless headphones. The feature, known as “TV Audio Swap,” is easy to set up and works seamlessly. It allowed me to watch late-night movies and live NBA games without disturbing those around me.

The revamped Sonos app is much better and easier to navigate than the previous edition. Its learning curve is minimal compared to before, and it brings a host of thoughtful extra touches. My favorite is the addition of Live Activities to the iOS app, which lets me access playback and volume controls directly from my iPhone’s lock screen or by long-pressing the Dynamic Island.

And, as ever, one of the biggest advantages of Sonos is its modular wireless connectivity, which allows you to build out a whole-home audio system over time. A soundbar can turn into a proper surround-sound system by adding a Sonos Sub Mini and a pair of Era 100 rear surround speakers for a full private-theater sound experience. And a home theater system can turn into audio for the whole house if you add more speakers in other rooms.

There is an obvious customer for the Sonos Beam Ultra: a discerning audiophile/home theater devotee with limited space who wants to compromise on quality as little as possible. This is a noticeable upgrade over just about any compact soundbar, and it may sound better than many full-size models, too. It’s very powerful, just as acoustically proficient, and offers processing features that I generally associate with larger bars.

As impressive as this is, the Arc Ultra remains the best Sonos soundbar, though. With 14 onboard audio drivers, it's simply more capable than the Beam Ultra: You’re getting similar sound, but it’s bigger, punchier, and more expressive. If you have the room, it’s the option to beat. (And Sonos specifically recommends the Beam Ultra for 65-inch TVs and smaller. If you have a 75-inch TV or larger, Beam Ultra may not meet the spec.) Ultimately, the Beam Ultra is incredibly impressive, though, and should open the door for many upgraders who want something that sounds special but can’t or don’t want to break that four-figure price barrier.

Stefan is an award-winning consumer technology editor with over a decade of experience in reviewing gadgets, particularly smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, desktop and laptop computers across multiple form factors and platforms, as well as accessories for them. He also covers televisions and audio equipment, including headphones, earbuds, wireless speakers, and soundbars. Since joining Hearst in 2015, Stefan has contributed to BestProducts, Popular Mechanics, and numerous other publications. Prior to his current role, he served as the US Editor for GSMArena.com.

#6295. Rising seas could threaten coastal homes sooner than flood maps suggest

A study of Oʻahu finds that waves and erosion could threaten homes, roads, and sewage systems earlier than simple sea level rise maps suggest.

Most sea level rise maps assume that only land below the future ocean level will flood.

A new study of Oʻahu found that this approach misses 62% to 73% of the land at risk when sea levels rise by less than 4 feet (1.2 meters).

Anna Mikkelsen, a graduate student in the Department of Earth Sciences at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, led the study, which was carried out with colleagues at the university’s Climate Resilience Collaborative.

Waves and coastal erosion could threaten homes, roads, and sewage systems on the Hawaiian island long before rising water floods these areas.

The researchers used computer models to estimate exposure rather than actual damage. They assumed that no new defenses would be built and that no buildings or residents would move between 2022 and 2150.

Planners often use a method called passive flooding in regions where little data is available.

The model raises the sea surface and marks land below the projected water level.

Mikkelsen’s team combined two other hazards with passive flooding. The team used an erosion model to project shoreline retreat along 9,523 survey lines around the island.

A separate wave model estimated coastal flooding from the largest waves of a typical year.

The three hazard maps were placed over public records of buildings, land parcels, roads, schools, hospitals, parks, sewer mains, and cesspools.

The researchers repeated the comparison at 1-foot (0.3-meter) increments of sea level rise, up to 6 feet (1.8 meters).

The dates for each step came from federal sea level projections issued in 2022 for the Honolulu tide gauge.

Under the Intermediate scenario, the sea stands 3.8 feet (1.16 meters) above its 2000 level by 2100.

Under the Intermediate-High scenario, which assumes rapid loss of ice sheets, it stands 5.8 feet (1.78 meters) above that level.

The ocean already reaches some of the island’s buildings.

In 2022, 544 buildings housing about 2,700 residents lay within zones exposed to erosion, high tides, or yearly high waves.

Passive flood maps would have missed nearly all 544 buildings. Waves alone affected 84% of them, while erosion affected the remaining 16%.

Passive flood maps also miss most threatened cesspools. Of the 54 cesspools already lying inside a hazard zone, 82% are threatened by erosion and 98% are left off passive flood maps.

On Oʻahu, waves and erosion threaten coastal areas before permanent flooding does.

The higher waterline is expected to become the main hazard after 3 to 4 feet of sea level rise.

The team estimates that 74% of the affected buildings and 87% of the affected cesspools would still be left off a passive map even when the sea has been raised by 4 feet.

“This tells us that it is critical to use multiple hazard models, and that areas with little data, such as other Pacific Islands, that rely on simpler passive flood model estimates may be underestimating the risk to their coastal infrastructure,” said Mikkelsen.

Exposure increases gradually through the first 3 feet (0.9 meters) of sea level rise. It then roughly doubles over the next foot.

The models project that the number of affected buildings goes from about 5,900 to about 11,100 between 3 and 4 feet of rise. Affected residents go from about 27,800 to 58,100 on an island of roughly 1 million people.

The length of affected road grows from 57 miles (92 kilometers) to 130 miles (210 kilometers). Affected sewer mains grow from 38 miles (61 kilometers) to 94 miles (151 kilometers).

The timing depends on the scenario. Sea levels are projected to rise 3 feet by 2073 under the Intermediate-High scenario and 4 feet by 2102 under the Intermediate scenario.

“Sea-level rise will not come to O‘ahu as a slow, harmless rise in the water level,” said Chip Fletcher, the paper’s senior author and director of the Climate Resilience Collaborative.

“Waves and erosion are already damaging homes, roads and wastewater systems, and our results show a threshold, somewhere between 0.9 and 1.2 meters of rise, where scattered local problems become widespread infrastructure failure.”

Honolulu has the largest number of exposed buildings and residents, and low streets in parts of the city are already flooded by high tides.

Honolulu’s dense street network gives drivers other routes around flooded blocks. But many rural coastal communities depend on a single highway.

The models project that erosion will make about 650 feet (200 meters) of Kamehameha Highway impassable in Kaʻaʻawa on the east side.

The models project this loss at just 1 foot of sea level rise, expected around 2051 under the Intermediate scenario. No alternative route runs along that shore.

Residents who live north of Kaʻaʻawa now reach central Honolulu in about 35 minutes, and that travel time would be tripled by a detour around the rest of the island.

Farrington Highway carries as many as 40,000 vehicles a day along the west side, and no public alternative exists for it.

Impassable sections are projected by the models at 3 feet of rise and 15% of the highway is projected to be impassable at 4 feet.

Earlier studies of managed retreat in Hawaii put the cost of relocating a major road and its buried utilities at about $279,210 per meter in 2025 dollars.

The authors applied that figure to the 31 miles (50 kilometers) of major road exposed by 2100. The estimated cost came to nearly $14 billion.

Many households on Oʻahu are not connected to a sewer and send their wastewater into one of the island’s roughly 8,000 cesspools.

A cesspool is an unlined pit that releases untreated sewage into the surrounding soil. A 2017 state law requires all cesspools to be phased out by 2050.

The number of cesspools inside a hazard zone is projected by the models to rise from 54 in 2022 to 92 at 1 foot of sea level rise and to 738 at 4 feet.

Cesspools and septic systems already leak sewage into coastal waters around Oʻahu. This pollution damages coral reefs and increases the risk of waterborne illness.

“These pathways would increase as sea levels rise because the groundwater also rises, and these systems may become flooded or unable to function properly,” Mikkelsen said.

The central sewer network also faces risks. High tides already push contaminated water from the Ala Wai Canal through Honolulu’s storm drains and into its streets.

The models project that the number of affected sewage pump stations could rise from one today to 16 after 4 feet of sea level rise.

The main threat also varies from one coast to another.

In Honolulu, passive flooding and wave flooding account for most exposure. Erosion accounts for roughly half on the North Shore, while yearly high waves dominate along the Waiʻanae coast in the west.

A building was counted as affected whenever any part of its footprint was touched by a hazard zone.

This approach shows which buildings face flooding or erosion. It does not measure how badly each building might be damaged.

The models also left out rainfall, storms, sinking land, and rising groundwater.

Groundwater already floods some basements in Honolulu, but the maps do not show these buildings as affected until sea levels rise by 6 feet. For this reason, the authors say their estimates may be too low.

Another modeling assumption could overstate erosion risk.

The erosion model did not account for seawalls and other barriers that line 27% to 29% of Oʻahu’s sandy shoreline, so it may overstate erosion wherever those structures continue to hold.

The researchers also did not examine how the three hazards affect one another.

They ran each model independently, so the flood models retained the current shoreline even where the erosion model projected beach loss.

The University of Hawaiʻi has made every hazard layer public in its SOEST Climate Viewer. These results update estimates from a 2017 state report on sea level rise used by state and county planners.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research: Climate.

#6294. After 40 Years, Scientists Finally Detect Evidence of an Almost Impossible Particle Decay

Evidence of a rare particle decay fits physics’ best theory, giving scientists a new way to test whether our understanding of matter leaves something out.

After more than 40 years of searching, physicists have found the first evidence of a particle decay predicted to occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The signal, recorded by the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC), offers a way to look for undiscovered particles through the influence they might have on that exceptionally unlikely event.

Inside the protons and neutrons at an atom’s center are smaller building blocks called up and down quarks. Beauty quarks are heavier members of the same family, produced in huge numbers when particles collide at the LHC, and they exist for only around one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying. LHCb studies particles containing these short-lived quarks. In the decay at the center of the new result, known as Bd to mu mu, one such particle transforms into two muons, particles similar to electrons but heavier.

With a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma, the signal is strong enough to qualify as evidence of the decay, although more data will be needed to reach the five-sigma threshold required to claim a discovery in particle physics.

Professor Chris Parkes, head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, said, “This decay is remarkably unlikely, the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.”

An undiscovered particle could change the chances of a beauty particle decaying in a particular way, giving physicists a means of detecting its influence even if they cannot observe it directly at the LHC. The rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to such effects. Researchers can therefore look for discrepancies between the measured decay rate and the predictions of the Standard Model, their best current theory of fundamental particles and their interactions. The new measurement matches those predictions, and greater precision could help reveal where the theory might eventually begin to break down.

By pursuing these increasingly precise measurements, physicists hope to probe what they call the “Zeptoverse,” an unexplored world at distances of a zeptometer, or a billionth of a trillionth of a meter, where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, deputy physics coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, said, “There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.

“The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.”

Just five millimeters, or about 0.2 inches, from the LHC beams sits the Vertex Locator, a silicon pixel detector that tracks the paths of particles emerging from collisions with extreme precision. This major UK-built component is part of the upgraded LHCb experiment. University of Manchester researchers played key roles in the experiment and its upgrade, including developing detector technology that helped make the measurement possible.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who led construction of the detectors at the University of Manchester, said, “We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.”

Parkes led the international LHCb collaboration through construction of the upgrade and led its approval of the new result. Made a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year for his work on LHCb, he said, “The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking – a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

“The UK made the largest nation contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today’s result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start, we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.”

By collecting data at up to five times its previous rate, the upgraded experiment is expected to build a much larger dataset into the early 2030s. A further planned upgrade could increase that rate by another factor of ten, enabling more precise measurements of these decays and increasing sensitivity to undiscovered particles at even shorter distances.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who was not involved in the experiment, said, “This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don’t understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing – that’s science! LHCb is a major scientific success.”

The experiment is funded by the Science and Technology Facilities Council as part of UK Research and Innovation.

#6293. Just like humans, orangutans prefer experiences they learned about while hearing laughter because it puts them in a good mood

Orangutans preferred a reward associated with laughter a day after learning about it, suggesting mood may shape what they value later.

Grandma’s pancakes may taste especially good because of the happy moments associated with them. Our mood during an experience can influence how much we value it later.

Now the same thing has turned up in orangutans, the least social of the great apes.

In a zoo test, six orangutans learned to dig a nut out of one material right after hearing other orangutans laugh. They learned to find a nut in a second material after hearing wind.

Both materials offered the same reward, yet a day after the last lesson, the apes preferred the material associated with laughter.

Daan Laméris, a postdoctoral researcher at Indiana University, led the work with Erica Cartmill, a professor at IU Bloomington.

Five of the orangutans live at ZOO Planckendael in Belgium, where Laméris ran most of the sessions, and the sixth lives at the Indianapolis Zoo.

Six animals is a small group, as ape studies usually are. And the good mood is the researchers’ reading of what the apes chose, since an orangutan can’t say how it feels.

In an interview with Earth.com, Cartmill said her lab’s earlier studies had already given evidence that hearing laughter puts apes in a positive mood.

“For me, the most important take-away from our study is that emotions influence learning,” she said. “In particular, if an orangutan is in a more positive mood when they learn something new, they will value that thing more strongly.”

On each trial, the experimenter set two plywood platforms in front of an orangutan.

Each held a bowl of a different material, shredded paper and yarn, for example, and an almond or a cashew was buried in one of the bowls, out of sight.

Once an ape pushed a finger into one bowl, the other platform was pulled away.

The apes learned two pairings over four days. The nut was always under one material on days one and three, and under a new material on days two and four.

A session ended once an ape chose right six times in a row, or after 30 trials.

Before each session, the ape spent five minutes beside two speakers, encouraged to stay nearby through familiar care routines and a bit of fruit every 10 to 15 seconds.

Ahead of one pairing, the apes heard laughter and play squeaks recorded from young orangutans they had never met. Ahead of the other, they heard wind noise at the same volume.

On day five, the two rewarded materials came back together for 30 trials. A nut was hidden under each on a random third of them, so the apes had nothing new to learn.

All six orangutans chose the laughter-paired material more often than the wind-paired one. For four of the six, the preference was strong enough that chance is an unlikely explanation.

On average, the apes picked the laughter-paired material on about two out of every three choices.

Unlike the other great apes, orangutans don’t live in stable groups. They meet up now and then in temporary parties, so they have fewer chances than chimpanzees, bonobos, or gorillas to hear another ape laugh.

Cartmill’s lab had already found that bonobos responded more optimistically to ambiguous situations after hearing laughter, in a 2025 study. Orangutans looked like the harder case.

“It is surprising to find these effects with orangutans, because they are the least social of all the great apes,” Laméris said. “So even among relatively non-social animals, laughter is important.”

Laméris told Earth.com that the result suggests the effect of positive social signals on thinking may run deeper in great apes than their social lives alone would predict.

“It also highlights that being relatively solitary doesn’t mean being socially or emotionally insensitive,” he said.

Before the laughter test, the team checked that the task could detect value at all. The routine was the same five days, but one material hid three nuts and the other hid one.

Four of the six apes later preferred the three-nut material, and the group as a whole did too. With six animals, though, the statistics behind that check were less firm than the laughter result.

The check matters because it shows what a preference in this task means. The apes’ choices on day five tracked how much a hiding place had been worth to them.

The preference associated with laughter was comparable in size to the preference associated with a larger reward.

Neither laughter nor the bigger reward made the apes learn faster. They reached six correct choices in a row at about the same pace whichever sound they had heard and whatever the payout.

What did speed them up was practice, since second sessions went faster than first ones.

The findings suggest that laughter influenced how much the apes valued what they had learned, without changing how quickly they learned it.

People show the same pattern, and it hadn’t been tested in another great ape before.

Laughter spreads between people, and great apes copy each other’s play faces and play sounds. Yet none of the orangutans laughed in response to the recordings.

“One important finding of our study is that the orangutans did not start laughing themselves after hearing play vocalizations,” Laméris said.

“While laughter can be contagious in humans, we did not observe this.”

The shift happened without any visible copying, the authors wrote. Feeling along with another animal and mirroring its expression usually happen together, and this result pulls them apart.

Orangutans do catch each other’s yawns and scratching, so they aren’t immune to copying. Here, though, the effect showed up in their choices rather than in laughter or other visible mimicry.

Laméris said the method is a way to study feelings in animals that can’t report them.

Rather than relying only on visible behavior, researchers can measure how an experience changes what an animal later chooses.

That approach, he said, could lead to better ways of assessing animal welfare.

The researchers adapted a test originally developed for rats, whose later choices can shift after play sessions or tickling by a handler.

Whether five minutes of recorded laughter changes how an orangutan learns anything outside a test, or how well it lives, is an open question.

Laméris said the team doesn’t know yet whether the effect carries over to everyday learning or welfare, though an environment that promotes positive states “is likely to enhance learning, and more broadly improve the welfare of animals.”

The group is part of a larger project on joy in animals. Laméris said a study of how laughter changes what chimpanzees pay attention to is already complete.

Cartmill said a version of the orangutan test is now under way with pet dogs.

Those results could help reveal whether the effect extends to animals more distantly related to humans.

The full study was published in the journal Biology Letters.

#6292. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6291. These 1,500-Year-Old Warriors Were Buried With Riches. Their Wounds Paint a Darker Picture.

The rare cemetery could finally shed light on a shadowy era after Rome’s collapse in what is now France.

Archaeologists with the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap) were excavating ahead of a residential construction project near Colmar, on the banks of the Ill River in eastern France. According to a translated statement, they found both a Gallo-Roman village occupied from the first to the third century C.E., and a fifth-century funerary complex containing 14 human burials and two horse burials.

The human burials included 11 adults or older adolescents and three children. Human bone fragments found west of the necropolis suggest that more burials may lie beyond the site’s boundaries. The burial pits were typically quadrangular or trapezoidal in shape and sized to fit the person buried inside. Some of the pits were also filled with artifacts.

Those artifacts caught the archaeologists’ attention. Two graves contained high-quality goods associated with warriors, including a sword partially preserved in a wooden scabbard, a single-edged knife, a shield, and a barbed javelin. The Inrap experts said the grave goods match those of Germanic chieftains, whose peoples allied with and joined the Roman army in the region near the Empire’s Rhine frontier during the fifth century.

The weapons and the clothing both featured decorative elements made of gold and silver and inlaid with garnets, further evidence of the high status of those buried.

Two graves associated with women also produced impressive finds, including silver-gilt bow brooches, silver bird-shaped brooches, glass-bead necklaces, belt buckles, and a bone comb. Even the horses received grave goods: harness equipment was buried with both animals.

The skeletons, however, told a grimmer story, with signs of injury and poor health found throughout the 14 burials. At least two of the deceased had fractures that were never set, and one of these likely left a man’s lower leg useless. Two other individuals had bone injuries likely caused by edged weapons. “The complete absence of perilesional bone remodeling suggests that death followed these violent acts rapidly,” the experts wrote.

The team was surprised to find so many injuries linked to violence in such a small sample of burials.

The fifth-century funerary complex was the excavation’s most striking discovery, but it wasn’t the only one. The team also uncovered part of the Gallo-Roman village’s core, including a residential district and a network of streets, showing that people lived there continuously from the first to the third century C.E.

Human activity at the site began in the middle of the first century C.E., and the site was most densely occupied from the second into the third century. Houses built of perishable materials stood on stone footings and were arranged along a street network that changed over time. Archaeologists also found hearths and wells, along with other structures that they said may have been used for industrial work.

After the village declined, a layer of silt covered the area. The silt shows only occasional use and little human activity through the fourth century, until the burials appeared in the fifth century.

Because evidence from this era is so rare, the funerary complex helps shed light on the poorly understood transition between the end of the Western Roman Empire and the Merovingian era in the Alsace region. “The exceptional nature of this find stems, in particular, from the scarcity of sites that document Germanic settlements during the specific chronological period in the region,” the statement reads. “These new findings will undoubtedly provide a fresh impetus for examining the region’s settlement dynamics, as well as the profound upheavals that shaped this territory during the second half of the fifth century.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold bear would have been worn on a headdress.

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The 2,200-year-old gold bear is a unique find in Kazakhstan.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.

Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan excavated a 2,200-year-old burial mound.

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.

It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

Archaeologists found a surprising number of human bones in the burial mound.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."

After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.
