#6289. Strange new material pulses in perfect rhythm to make future robots feel more alive

Dozens of motorized cells that start vibrating at random merge into one slow pulse, forming a mechanical time crystal that holds its rhythm.

A few musicians can hold a beat together, but an orchestra with no conductor tends to drift apart. Physicists have now built a sheet of material that does the opposite, and ends up making unified waves.

Nudge it, and dozens of small motorized cells begin to twitch on their own, each at its own pace. Over a few seconds the twitches merge into one slow pulse that the whole sheet keeps, and there’s no clock telling it when.

The team at the University of Amsterdam and the University of Birmingham calls the merging process wave coarsening.

The final state is what physicists call a time crystal: matter that repeats a motion in time the way an ordinary crystal repeats a pattern in space.

“Our research provides a striking example of spontaneous organization – tiny vibrations organizing themselves until an entire material moves in a coordinated way,” said Jack Binysh of Birmingham, a co-lead author who began the work in Amsterdam.

“Like musicians gradually finding the same beat, individual parts of an active material can organize their movements until the whole structure moves together.”

Each cell of the material is a trio of elastic hexagons wired to a small circuit board. A sensor reads how each hexagon is squeezed, and a voice-coil actuator, the kind found in a loudspeaker, pushes on it.

The board follows one rule. When a hexagon is compressed, its clockwise neighbor is compressed too, and its counterclockwise neighbor is stretched.

The rule breaks a symmetry that ordinary materials obey. Push on a spring and it pushes back the same way whichever end you push.

These cells respond differently depending on direction, which physicists call non-reciprocal. They can only do it because each one has its own power.

The team built 37 of these cells into a honeycomb and set it on a glass plate slicked with Teflon so it could slide freely. Then they turned the pushback strength past the point where a single cell starts to oscillate on its own.

Given a shake, each cell began vibrating at about 30 times a second. Then something slower took over.

A longer wave crept around the edge of the material in one direction, growing in wavelength, in period, and in size, until it drowned out the fast twitching. A few seconds in, every cell was shearing back and forth together on one steady rhythm.

The team ran the experiment six times, each from a different random jolt. Each time, the distance over which cells moved in step grew by a power law while the vibration’s energy rose.

A mathematical model of the sheet reproduced the same growth on a line and on a grid. In the model, energy is pumped in without pushing or spinning the sheet as a whole.

The last step is what makes the words time crystal apply.

In simulations, the team subjected the final oscillation to noise. The larger the sheet, the longer its rhythm held, a sign that the order survives at scale rather than being washed out by small disturbances.

To check that the effect was not a quirk of one design, the team built a second material. It was an elastic ring carrying 24 small torque motors that twist in response to their neighbors, floated on an air table.

Any small disturbance of the material set off short waves around the ring, which merged into longer ones.

The ring’s shapes took turns. A six-lobed pattern grew first and briefly dominated, then a five-lobed one caught up and overtook it, then four, each dying as the next longer shape took over.

In the end the ring settled into a slow cycle around a flattened, pancake-like shape.

“Wave coarsening could be exploited as a way of controlling shape changes and directed motion – proving useful in robotics, active matter and optomechanics,” Binysh said.

“Our discovery could form a key step towards the development of biology-inspired multifunctional robots.”

The coarsening stops if the material can push against something. When the team removed the Teflon so the honeycomb rubbed on the glass, the short waves kept circling and never merged into the whole-sheet pulse.

In the model, friction sets the wavelength at which the waves get stuck.

The team also simulated a much larger disc of 5,813 cells. There, coarsening started everywhere at once, but waves along the rim soon took over.

They ran in one direction around the edge, the way currents run around the edge of certain quantum materials.

On a ring-shaped disc, the inner and outer edges carried waves in opposite directions and, with friction added, the two stayed at the edges instead of invading the middle.

Both the model and the simulations of growing size confirmed the time crystal. The physical sheets of material had 37 and 24 cells. The honeycomb is flat and only shears.

What wave coarsening does in a three-dimensional material that can bend and twist is untested, and that is what the team wants to build next.

The applied question is whether one material can hold several stable rhythms and switch between them. Co-lead author Jonas Veenstra, now at ENS de Lyon, said the group has started to think about it.

Each pattern could get a different job, such as a shape change or a direction of travel, and a single material could then do the work of several machines.

Such a material would be a step toward robots that coordinate the way flocks and fireflies do, with no central controller, a direction the Amsterdam group has already explored.

Corentin Coulais leads that group, with Anton Souslov of the University of Cambridge as co-corresponding author and co-authors at Delft University of Technology and Leiden University. The materials, Coulais said, carried more than 100 sensors and actuators.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6288. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6287. AI Surveillance Could Be Harming Your Health. Here’s How.

Doctors from Harvard and Johns Hopkins warn that mass surveillance is a health hazard—and AI is making it much worse.

When CEOs and scientists wax poetic about the potential benefits of AI, the technology’s impact on human health often rises to the top—and in many ways, they’re not wrong. Artificial intelligence’s ability to sift through massive datasets makes these algorithms ideal for spotting early-stage cancer or discovering novel drugs. The United Nations even notes that AI-powered disease surveillance could detect potential outbreaks quickly and prevent crises from spiraling into global pandemics.

However, like any tool, artificial intelligence can also be used for nefarious purposes, and a new perspective published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights a particularly insidious one and its potential impacts on human health: mass surveillance. Debates over how governments and companies collect our personal data are usually framed as civil liberties or national security issues. But experts from Massachusetts General Hospital, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, and Harvard Medical School say that being watched can make us sick, and in the age of AI, things could get much, much worse.

The authors identify at least three ways surveillance harms health. First, knowing (or even believing) that you’re constantly being monitored can lead to hypervigilance and chronic “anticipatory stress,” which takes a toll on both physical and mental health. Second, surveillance can scare vulnerable people away from essential health behaviors. This includes groups with a reasonable fear of persecution, such as undocumented immigrants or people seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care, who may avoid pharmacies and clinics, hold back details from their doctors, or even skip buying groceries. Third, surveillance data can be used to hand out things that shape our health, like insurance, housing, and jobs, unequally.

“Historically, mass surveillance programs in the United States have most often been organized by government agencies and subject to democratic oversight,” the authors write. “AI-enabled surveillance, however, relies on data ecosystems that are controlled primarily by private companies.”

That’s a big distinction. The Fourth Amendment’s protections are limited when people voluntarily share information with third parties, even if they don’t realize they’re doing so. HIPAA also generally doesn’t cover data collected by consumer-facing tech companies. As a result, AI companies and other private actors can access and analyze vast amounts of personal data, and they could share it with the government without your knowledge or permission. Traditional surveillance usually needed human oversight. AI, by contrast, can continuously comb through social media, search results, financial transactions, geolocation records, and camera footage, then combine it all into increasingly powerful predictions.

This concern isn’t without real-world precedent. The Denver-based Palantir Technologies, founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, developed AI-enabled tools for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), including a system known as ImmigrationOS. ICE has used these tools to combine information from multiple government databases, including visa histories and Medicaid records, to target people for immigration enforcement. Another tool, called Enhanced Leads Identification and Targeting for Enforcement (ELITE), pulls names, photos, addresses, and race and ethnicity data from Medicaid records to map areas with people who could be detained, according to reporting in The BMJ. It can reportedly even generate a “confidence score” for whether someone might be at home.

For the authors, all this surveillance amounts to a public health problem. When data collected for health care or social services can be repurposed for surveillance, trust erodes, and people may stop using vital programs. That’s why they argue that AI-enabled mass surveillance should be considered an emerging “structural determinant of health,” which they define as a social, political, environmental, or economic condition that shapes how health and illness are distributed across a population.

“We believe medicine has an urgent responsibility to confront these developments,” the authors write. “Decisions about AI-enabled mass surveillance are being made with limited input from health experts, even though these systems have clear consequences for population health.” Health care technologies can contribute to the problem, too. Clinicians increasingly recommend wearables and smartphone apps that continuously collect patient data, which means the medical system may be feeding the same data streams that could be used for surveillance.

The courts offer another option. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with ICE and Palantir, and the authors say health care institutions can support these lawsuits by publicly opposing troubling data-sharing deals. Clinicians can also help by documenting patients’ fears about how their data is used and any resulting changes in whether they seek care, which gives litigators and policymakers evidence to work with.

AI surveillance could still be a boon to public health. The same ability to rapidly pull together data from different sources that makes it dangerous could also help health officials spot and respond to threats more effectively. In the end, AI is just a tool, and it’s up to us how we use it. But the authors warn that we may not have long to decide. By the time AI surveillance’s effects become fully apparent, its infrastructure “may already be deeply embedded in everyday life.” As they put it, “The norms established today could determine whether AI-enabled surveillance becomes a tool in service to population health or a driver of avoidable health inequities and structural harm.”

#6286. Almost all of Europe’s wild bee species still exist, but their shrinking habitats tell a much darker story

A century of records shows European pollinator decline is uneven. Nearly all wild bee species persist, but most have lost range since 1921.

At first glance, the survival of Europe’s wild bees looks like a success story. Records show that almost every bee species seen in the last century is still alive somewhere today.

However, when scientists map out exactly where these bees are actually living, it becomes clear that their territories are rapidly disappearing.

Most wild bee species occupy less of Europe than they did a century ago. Among the species with enough records to track, the average bee has lost about a third of its range since 1921.

The authors call it a reshuffling rather than an extinction wave: sensitive species are thinning out while a resilient few spread.

Carlos Martínez-Núñez of the Doñana Biological Station in Sevilla, part of Spain’s national research council, CSIC, led the analysis.

His co-authors include Ignasi Bartomeus at Doñana, who designed the study with him, and researchers at the University of Mons in Belgium and the University of Novi Sad in Serbia.

The records they used were gathered opportunistically over a century, not in a planned survey. They come from museum drawers, expert collections, published papers and online databases.

So the team had to correct for a century of uneven collecting, and it could estimate trends for only about 40 percent of species.

The dataset holds more than four million records of wild bees and hoverflies collected across Europe between 1921 and 2020, each one checked by taxonomists.

Hoverflies are flower-visiting flies and Europe’s other big group of insect pollinators.

Between them, the records cover 1,898 wild bee species and 784 hoverfly species. That’s 88 percent of the 3,051 known on the continent.

To turn scattered records into trends, the team divided Europe into hexagonal cells with sides about 31 miles (50 kilometers) long.

For each species and each year, the models estimated which cells it occupied. They also estimated how likely a species was to be recorded at all, so a decade with few collectors wouldn’t read as a decade with few bees.

About 91 percent of the species in the dataset have at least one record from 2001 onward. The rest, at most 9 percent, could be candidates for extinction across the continent.

However, most of them were extremely rare a century ago too, and the IUCN’s European Red Lists name only 14 bee species and one hoverfly as possibly extinct.

Counting species, region by region, gave a mostly stable picture as well. The Atlantic region, which takes in the United Kingdom, Belgium, the Netherlands and western France, lost wild bee and hoverfly species steadily across the century.

In the Continental region of central and eastern Europe, the historical decline in bees slowed while hoverflies fell in recent decades.

Most of what scientists know about pollinator decline comes from the Atlantic region, where farmland was transformed over the past century. The authors wrote that declines that steep may not hold across the rest of Europe.

The species-by-species view is where the reassurance ends. In every region except the Alpine one, more bee species were shrinking their range than expanding it.

In an interview with Earth.com, Martínez-Núñez said that gap is what surprised him most, and that a count of species alone can hide big changes.

“Species may still be present, but their declining occupancy can provide an early warning of broader environmental change, long before they become extinct,” he said.

Averaged across Europe, bee occupancy fell by 0.42 percent a year, a 34 percent drop over the century.

For hoverflies, the pattern looked different: species expanding and contracting were roughly balanced, and the continental average rose.

“Hoverflies show a contrasting positive trend at the European scale, highlighting the importance of looking beyond broad generalizations about pollinator decline,” Martínez-Núñez told Earth.com.

But that rise came mostly from a small number of species with very large gains, and from the early decades, when records are thin. When the team began the analysis in 1971 instead, the hoverfly increase flattened to no change.

For bees, the later start changed where the losses showed up. The Atlantic decline disappeared, which fits damage done early by agricultural intensification. Declines in the cold Boreal north and the warm Mediterranean south grew steeper.

The Alpine region was the exception: declining bee species didn’t outnumber expanding ones there, and among hoverflies the expanding species dominated.

The authors read that as warm-adapted species moving uphill as the climate warms.

Body size, diet, social habits and climate preference together explained less than 1 percent of the variation in how a species did.

However, one weak pattern held. Bee species tied to warmer climates tended to expand their range, and cold-adapted groups, bumblebees among them, tended to contract, with wide differences inside each group. Hoverfly declines clustered in cold-adapted genera as well.

Some genera of parasitic bees, which lay their eggs in other bees’ nests, declined consistently, and so did some bees that collect pollen from a narrow group of plants. Others of the same kind did fine.

The team found a weak link between a parasitic species’ trend and its host’s.

The regions that worry Martínez-Núñez most are the Atlantic and Continental ones, where bee and hoverfly diversity has declined.

“I’m also concerned about specialist and parasitic bees, which may be particularly vulnerable to environmental change.”

Bee species the IUCN Red List classes as Critically Endangered showed the steepest declines of all.

Species the list marks as Data Deficient, meaning too poorly known to assess, also had consistently low trends. The authors took that as a sign that little-studied species may be declining without anyone noticing.

Occupancy tracks where a species is found, not how many individuals live there. A bee could be vanishing from most of a cell and still count as present. The models worked for 1,225 of the roughly 1,940 species with enough records to try.

Records are sparse in the first half of the century studied. Some regions have thin coverage, and the recent downturn in Alpine hoverflies shifted when the team changed the model, so they called it too early to confirm.

Whether the reshuffling is already costing Europe pollination is the open question. The authors wrote that the consequences of this kind of species turnover are rarely tested.

Asked what can be done now, Martínez-Núñez said farmers can keep hedgerows, field margins and flower-rich habitats. City planners can link up green spaces planted with native species.

“Gardeners can plant native flowers that bloom throughout the year and avoid pesticides,” said Martínez-Núñez.

The authors expect their trend data to feed the next Red List assessments, including for pollinators now listed as of Least Concern that are in decline.

Long-term monitoring of Europe’s wild pollinators is still missing, so a century of museum drawers is the only long view there is.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6285. A Viking Couple’s Grave May Reveal Who Really Settled This Strategic Island 1,100 Years Ago

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man were surprised to find not one but two of the island’s most significant Viking finds.

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man received double the surprise when they uncovered a 1,100-year-old double grave. It contained rare brooches typically worn by Scandinavian women and a sword that, according to one expert, would once have gleamed with a “bright silver” pommel. The site also produced intricately decorated trading weights, a Viking axe head, balance scales, and a ceremonial bronze ladle.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” Allison Fox said in a statement. Fox is curator for archaeology at Manx National Heritage, a museum and heritage trust on the Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland. “What makes it particularly exciting is the combination of finds, which gives us a rare opportunity to explore the lives of some of the island’s earliest Scandinavian settlers.”

Experts believe the metal detectorists, Daniel Crowe and Rhett Britton, came upon the double grave of a man and a woman who were buried with some of their finest possessions: three brooches for her and a sword for him. Fox said the date of the brooches suggests the grave may be the “earliest known female Viking Age burial” on the island. Together with the other finds, she said, the objects “help us build a picture of the people who lived here more than a thousand years ago, how they traded, and the connections they maintained across the Viking world.”

The find dates to around 900 C.E. That places it at the early end of the Viking Age on the Isle of Man, just as Scandinavian communities were becoming established there. Some of the objects are also the first of their kind found on the island.

Museum experts believe the Vikings first arrived on the island during the ninth century. Recognizing the strategic importance of its location in the Irish Sea, they established trading links before settling there. A rich Viking heritage remains across the island, and burials found in the past show evidence of pagan traditions. Viking influence still runs through Manx culture today. Tynwald, the island’s parliament, was founded during the Viking Age and is known as one of the world’s oldest continuous parliaments.

After making their discovery, Crowe and Britton didn’t try to clean the objects. Fox says this has allowed experts to fully appreciate the objects’ intricate details. She added that the brooches still have soil inside them, and the team is carefully excavating it in hopes of finding traces of textile.

Two of the brooches are a matching pair of oval “tortoise” brooches, the kind Scandinavian women wore to fasten their dresses at the shoulders. Both are covered in intricate interlocking animals, a hallmark of Viking art. According to Manx National Heritage, only one other pair like them has ever been found on the Isle of Man, and that was found by Daniel Crowe’s own father, John Crowe, along with fellow metal detectorist Craig Evans. The new pair is likely about 50 years older, which is why experts think this grave may be the island’s earliest known female Viking burial. The third brooch, decorated with spirals and a glass center, is the first of its kind found on the island.

The sword is the type a man would have carried, and it’s the 13th Viking sword found on the Isle of Man. Although the blade is badly corroded and parts of it are missing entirely, Fox said in a video from the heritage group that the pommel still shows “signs of the really intricate decorating that would have been on the pommel when it was buried.” X-ray analysis revealed traces of silver and copper wire inlaid into the iron, which makes it one of only three swords found on the island with such decoration.

“When this sword was buried,” she said, “this top part of the sword would have been really bright silver, a really high-status object.” In addition, traces of wood show that the sword’s handle was covered in wood rather than thread or horn.

Although 1,100 years in the ground caused much of the sword’s damage, experts believe the Vikings broke it on purpose as part of a burial ritual.

Because the brooches were found alongside the sword (items linked to a woman and a man, respectively), a double burial seems likely. Experts said, however, that they can’t be sure whether the grave goods came from one grave or from two graves placed close together.

Beyond the burial itself, the decorated lead weights and bronze balance scales found at the site highlight the Isle of Man’s role in Irish Sea trade. The weights are the first of their kind found on the island. One of them has a decorative bronze fitting, with artwork typical of Britain and Ireland, that may have been taken from another object.

The bronze ladle, another first for the island, was likely used in ceremonies.

Despite all the experts have gleaned from the discovery, there’s still much to be learned. “Although the original burial site has been disturbed,” Fox said, “further research may reveal much more about these objects and the people who owned them.”

#6284. Ocean research has a data problem, but a new tool could help

Free software called oceandatr brings scattered ocean datasets together, helping marine scientists prepare maps and plan conservation research.

Information about water depth and underwater mountains around a Pacific island may already exist, but finding and combining it can be difficult.

For a marine scientist, finding it and getting it into a usable form can take as much effort as the research it was supposed to support.

A new free software package brings those scattered datasets together with one command. In one test, it assembled the data for a Pacific conservation planning exercise in a little over two minutes.

The package is called oceandatr. Jason Flower, a project scientist at the Environmental Markets Lab at the University of California, Santa Barbara, led the work.

Colleagues at the University of Queensland, the Waitt Institute, and four other institutions joined him.

“This paper is unique, in that we weren’t trying to answer a specific research question,” said co-author Echelle Burns, a project scientist at the lab.

“We were building a tool for marine scientists like us, who find themselves using the same data-pulling and organizing workflow over and over again.”

The ocean’s measurements sit on many websites, run by many groups.

Seafloor depth comes from one international compilation, and the locations of underwater mountains from a separate catalog.

Maps of coral habitat come from another source. Records of where boats fish come from Global Fishing Watch, which tracks them by satellite.

Each source stores its data at a different scale and in a different format.

Before any of it can go on the same map, a researcher has to download it, trim it to the area of interest, and reshape it so the grids match.

Flower and his colleagues had written that code so many times that they turned their scripts into ready-made functions and published them.

The tool works in R, a programming language that environmental scientists already use widely. It asks for three things in order.

First, a boundary for the area of interest, which can be a country, an ocean, or the zone a nation controls offshore. Second, a grid laid over that boundary.

Third, the data, which the tool fetches from each source and drops into the grid.

Depth comes from the GEBCO global terrain model. The tool downloads it in chunks, so it can process datasets too large to load into memory all at once.

Smaller datasets that exist only as single global files, such as the seamount and coral maps, ride along in a companion package.

That way they don’t have to be downloaded again with every update.

“The package could be used in any marine science project that requires spatial data,” Flower said. Researchers can also feed in their own measurements, and the tool fits them to the same grid.

To show the tool working, the team drew a planning region in the high seas of the western Pacific. They cut it into 8,142 squares, each 6.2 miles (10 kilometers) across.

For every square, oceandatr gathered depth, seafloor landforms, seamounts, coral habitat, and environmental zones, along with how much fishing happened there during the year 2022.

On an ordinary desktop PC, that took 2 minutes and 16 seconds. That is the step that used to mean writing fresh code for every dataset.

The team then fed the result into a conservation planning tool that picks protected areas while keeping the cost to fishing low. The target was to set aside 20% of each habitat type.

In a second test, the team modeled where fishing happens across the waters of the Federated States of Micronesia, using seafloor depth, distance to port, sea temperature, and dissolved oxygen.

The model accounted for about half of the differences in fishing effort from place to place.

The authors wrote that it was a demonstration of the data pipeline, not a finished fisheries model. A rigorous one, they wrote, would go through a formal process of choosing which variables to keep.

The tool is only as good as the datasets behind it. The global depth map can be coarser than what a local survey holds, which is why the package lets a user swap in their own depth file instead.

The team built the tool partly through marine planning work with the Waitt Institute in small island nations.

Users must judge whether the global datasets provide enough detail to study an individual island’s reef. They can supply local data when finer detail is needed.

The code is public on GitHub. The authors plan to add daily sea surface temperature alongside the long-term averages, and to make the package run faster on older computers.

“R packages are constantly evolving, and oceandatr will evolve with them,” Burns said. “It’s a ‘living package’ that’s going to continue to be updated and refined in the coming years.”

The full study was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

Archaeologists have discovered the shoe of the first governor of the Danish West Indies, recovered from a 17th-century ship that was wrecked after one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark’s history.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Maritime archaeologists investigating a 17th-century shipwreck off the coast of Sweden have discovered a fancy shoe and two metal rings used as currency in the transatlantic slave trade. The items were lost during a mutiny on a slave ship in 1683, during which the governor of the Danish West Indies was thrown overboard.

The Danish frigate Havmanden (which translates to "Merman") was en route to St. Thomas, a Caribbean island that is now part of the U.S. Virgin Islands, with convicts and indentured servants aboard destined for work on the island with the Danish West India Company. The plan for the Havmanden, after dropping off the new colonists, was to sail to West Africa to buy enslaved Africans. But due to a shortage of food and water, several crewmembers and convicts aboard seized control of the ship near the Azores in the North Atlantic and began sailing it back to Copenhagen.

The mutineers shot the ship's captain and threw other officers ‪—‬ including Jørgen Iversen Dyppel, the first governor of the Danish West Indies ‪—‬ overboard in the English Channel. After the ship ran aground, the mutineers were tried for their crimes in Copenhagen and sentenced to death.

The story of the Havmanden is one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark's history, according to a Nov. 11 translated statement from the National Museum of Denmark. But now, underwater archaeologists are learning more about the fateful voyage from the wreck, which lies on the seabed just east of Gothenburg, Sweden.

Archaeological divers discovered the rear half of a man's "unusually fine" shoe in the wreckage, according to the statement.

"I see a great many shoes from shipwrecks, but I have never before seen a shoe of such high quality," Vivi Lena Andersen, director of the Rudersdal Museums in Denmark, said in the statement.

The sole has a high level of craftsmanship, Andersen said, which can be seen in the minuscule holes perforating the edge of the shoe. The regularity of the holes would have required tools and expertise that only the most skilled shoemakers had at the time. It was "undoubtedly an expensive and exclusive shoe that only the elite could afford to buy," Andersen said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Because the shoe was likely owned by an upper-class individual, experts think it could have belonged to Iversen, the Danish West Indies governor who was thrown overboard.

"The shoe testifies not only to Jørgen Iversen Dyppel's life and dramatic death, but also provides a personal point of entry into the larger story of the establishment of the Danish colonies in the West Indies and the widespread slave trade Denmark was a part of," Andreas Kallmeyer Bloch, a maritime archaeologist at the National Museum of Denmark's Center for Maritime and Underwater Cultural Heritage, said in the statement.

Additional clues to the Danish slave trade on board the Havmanden included two manillas, ring-shaped pieces of metal that were used as currency in West Africa. European merchants cast manillas from copper, brass or iron and traded them for enslaved people in West Africa, particularly along the coast of modern-day Nigeria. But manillas are rarely found in Scandinavia, according to the statement.

"The manillas add another layer to Havmanden's story and underscore the connection to the slave trade, which was a central part of Denmark's colonial activities in both the West Indies and on the west coast of Africa," Kallmeyer Bloch said.

Denmark continued to engage in the transatlantic slave trade for more than a century after the Havmanden sank. Although King Christian VII of Denmark-Norway banned the trade in 1792, slavery continued in the Danish West Indies until 1848, when hundreds of enslaved people revolted and were finally granted their freedom.

#6282. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”
